projectTitle: Brightleaf Fitness: One Definition of "Active Member," Start to Finish
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish build of a governed analytics engineering layer — Snowflake, dbt, Git/CI, and Airflow, for one fictional subscription fitness company, from three conflicting metrics to one trusted number.
businessContext:
**Brightleaf Fitness** is a fictional mid-size subscription fitness company: roughly 40 physical studio locations plus a mobile app, with members paying a monthly subscription. For years, Finance, Marketing, and Product have each queried the same legacy on-premises SQL Server database with their own hand-written "active member" logic — built by different people, years apart, with no shared definition. Every month, the three teams report three different active-member counts to leadership, sometimes off by thousands, and nobody fully trusts any of the three numbers anymore.

You've been brought in as an Analytics Engineer to fix this at the root — not by declaring one team's number "correct," but by building one governed, tested, documented, version-controlled semantic layer that all three teams query from going forward. This series follows that build end to end: from the first discovery meeting through a real production bug, and out the other side to a single trusted dashboard.
architectureSummary: By the end of this series, Brightleaf Fitness has: a nightly Python extraction, orchestrated by Airflow, that lands raw SQL Server data into Snowflake untouched; a dbt project with staging models (`stg_memberships`, `stg_billing`, `stg_locations`), one intermediate model (`int_active_members`) that defines "active member" exactly once, and mart models (`member_activity_mart`, `revenue_mart`) that every team actually queries; a suite of dbt tests — generic and a custom singular test — enforcing the business rule and catching a real join-fanout regression that was found and fixed mid-series; a GitHub Actions CI pipeline that blocks any pull request from merging if a model or test fails; and one Power BI semantic model, built directly on the governed marts, that replaced three teams' three separate, conflicting reports. Nothing here is more advanced than the tools taught earlier in this path — the point of this series is showing how dbt, Snowflake, Git/CI, and Airflow fit together on one real job, not introducing new tools.

lessons.title: Meeting Brightleaf: Why Three Teams Have Three Different "Active Member" Numbers
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: uncovering why Finance, Marketing, and Product each have their own conflicting definition of an "active member" before any modeling begins.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll build one governed semantic layer for a fictional mid-size subscription fitness company, **Brightleaf Fitness** — roughly 40 physical studio locations plus a mobile app, a legacy on-premises SQL Server database nobody has touched the core logic of in years, and three teams who each independently wrote their own SQL to answer what sounds like the simplest possible question: how many members do we actually have right now?

By the end of this series you'll have a nightly Python extraction orchestrated by Airflow, a Snowflake warehouse, a tested and documented dbt project, and new Power BI reports for all three teams — all built on one shared, version-controlled definition of "active member." This video starts where that kind of project always starts: not with a single line of SQL, but with a room full of people who are each confident their number is the correct one.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine three friends each measuring the same room to see how big it is. One used a tape measure, one used their own footsteps, and one used a piece of string they eyeballed against the wall. Now all three come back with a different answer for the size of the exact same room — and each of them is positive their measurement is right, because each one measured carefully, just using a different tool and a different starting point.

That's exactly what's happening at Brightleaf Fitness, except the "room" is their list of paying members. Finance counts them one way, Marketing counts them another way, and the app team counts them a third way — and every single month, their three numbers don't match. Nobody is lying and nobody made a mistake. They just never agreed, back at the very start, on what "measuring the room" was even supposed to mean.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the discovery phase of an analytics engineering engagement, and the symptom that gets you called in is almost always political before it's technical: three departments no longer trust any report, including their own, because the numbers never reconcile. Your job in this first conversation isn't to adjudicate whose SQL is "correct" — it's to resist the urge to fix anything yet and instead extract exactly how each team currently defines the metric, in enough detail to see where the definitions diverge. That divergence is almost never a bug; it's three reasonable business rules that were each written in isolation, years apart, by people solving a slightly different problem.

At Brightleaf, you'll find Finance's query counts anyone with a non-canceled subscription row, which overcounts members who paused their membership for a month but didn't cancel. Marketing's query counts anyone with app or check-in activity in the last 30 days, which undercounts loyal members who go to a physical studio but don't use the app, and overcounts someone who checked in once during a free trial and never converted. Product's query joins through a different membership table that was added later for the multi-location pilot program, and double-counts members who belong to more than one studio location under the old schema. None of the three is malicious or careless — each is internally consistent with a narrower question that team actually needed answered at the time it was written. Naming those three specific, real divergences in this meeting is the single most valuable thing you'll do all series, because every dbt model you build starting in later lessons exists to resolve exactly these edge cases in one place instead of three.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Walk in already knowing what you don't know

Before the meeting, write down the specific ambiguities hiding behind "our numbers don't match":

- Does a paused membership count as active?
- Does a free trial member count the same as a paying member?
- If someone holds memberships at two studio locations, do they count once or twice?
- Is "active" measured as of today, or as of the last day of the reporting month?
- Does the mobile app's own activity log count as membership evidence, or only the billing record?

## Step 2 — Interview each team separately before comparing notes

Dana Whitfield, Brightleaf's VP of Member Experience, called this meeting and opens it bluntly:

```
DANA: Finance told the board we had 61,200 active members last month.
      Marketing's campaign dashboard says 58,400. Product's retention
      dashboard says 64,900. Those are three different companies, not
      three views of one company. I need this fixed at the root, not
      patched for one more month.
```

Then pull each team's own definition, in their own words, with the SQL they're actually running:

```sql
-- Finance's definition (Marcus Yi, Director of Finance)
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT member_id)
FROM dbo.memberships
WHERE subscription_status <> 'canceled';
-- Marcus: "If they haven't canceled, they're active. Paused is not canceled."

-- Marketing's definition (Priya Nandakumar, Head of Growth Marketing)
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT member_id)
FROM dbo.checkins
WHERE checkin_date >= DATEADD(day, -30, GETDATE());
-- Priya: "Active means engaged. If you haven't shown up in 30 days,
--         you're not who we target with retention campaigns."

-- Product's definition (Jordan Lee, Head of Product)
SELECT COUNT(member_location_id)
FROM dbo.member_locations
WHERE is_active_flag = 1;
-- Jordan: "This came from the multi-location pilot. Every active
--          location membership counts, even if it's the same person."
```

## Step 3 — Name the real divergence out loud, in the room

```
YOU: So Marcus, a member who paused their membership this month but
     didn't cancel — counted active or not?
MARCUS: Active. Pausing isn't canceling.

YOU: Priya, same person — paused, no check-ins in 30 days?
PRIYA: Not active in my number. They're not engaged.

YOU: Jordan, a member who joined both the downtown and the uptown
     studio under one account — how many rows is that in your table?
JORDAN: ...Two. That's actually a known issue, we've never fixed it.
```

That exchange is the whole project in miniature: three reasonable rules, zero agreement, and one newly-discovered bug (the double-count) that nobody had written down anywhere before this meeting.

## Step 4 — Write the one-page "three definitions" artifact

```
BRIGHTLEAF FITNESS — ACTIVE MEMBER DEFINITION AUDIT

Finance (billing-based):     Any non-canceled subscription row.
                              Overcounts: paused members.
Marketing (engagement-based): Check-in or app activity in last 30 days.
                              Undercounts: loyal non-app studio visitors.
                              Overcounts: one-time trial check-ins.
Product (location-based):     Active member_locations row.
                              Overcounts: multi-location members (2x).

Agreement so far: NONE of the three numbers is simply "wrong" — each
answers a real question that team actually needed. The problem is
structural: no shared, written, tested definition exists anywhere.
```

Don't propose a fix yet — Lesson 2 turns this audit into a testable business rule everyone can sign off on.

## Step 5 — Flag the discovered bug separately from the definition disagreement

The multi-location double-count Jordan admitted to is not a matter of opinion — it's a defect in the current reporting, independent of which "active" definition eventually wins. Log it as its own item so it doesn't get lost inside the bigger definition debate:

```
DEFECT (not a definitional disagreement):
  Product's member_locations-based count double-counts any member
  holding memberships at more than one studio. Confirmed by Jordan
  Lee in the discovery meeting. Affects Product's dashboard today,
  independent of which active-member rule is eventually adopted.
  Owner: carried forward into the Lesson 2 definition's deduplication
  requirement.
```

Separating "things everyone has to agree on" from "things that are just broken" keeps the discovery conversation from turning into a debate about something that was never actually a matter of opinion.

None of the three is simply buggy; they're three narrow definitions built for three different original questions, which is exactly why a shared semantic layer is the right fix, not a patch to one team's query.

lessons.title: Turning "Fix Our Metrics" Into a Testable Definition
lessons.summary: Converting the three-definitions audit into one written, testable business rule for "active member" that all three teams sign off on before any pipeline gets built.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 1 gave you three real, conflicting definitions of "active member" and the specific edge cases behind each one — paused memberships, 30-day engagement windows, and duplicated multi-location rows. That audit explains the disagreement, but it doesn't resolve it. This video is where you turn "fix our metrics" into a single, precise, testable business rule: a written definition specific enough that a dbt test can later check it automatically, and specific enough that Finance, Marketing, and Product can each look at it and say yes, that's what we meant, or no, that's wrong — not just nod vaguely in a meeting.

This definition is the document every later technical decision in this series answers to. When the intermediate dbt model gets built, when the custom singular test gets written, when the eventual join-fanout bug gets debugged, all of it traces back to one sentence you're about to write down and get three signatures on.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the three friends who each measured the room differently? Now imagine you get all three of them in one room with one tape measure, and you all agree together: "an active member is someone whose membership hasn't been canceled, AND hasn't been paused for more than 30 days, AND only gets counted once even if they belong to two locations." That's one rule now, written down, that all three friends agree to use from now on.

The tricky part isn't agreeing it sounds fair — it's making the rule specific enough that a computer could check it automatically, the same way a recipe has to say "bake for 22 minutes at 350 degrees" instead of just "bake until done," so two different people baking the same cake get the same result every time.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A business rule that sounds reasonable in a meeting and a business rule that's actually implementable are two different artifacts, and the gap between them is where most "we agreed on a metric" projects quietly fail. The test is falsifiability: for every clause in the definition, you need a concrete data example where the rule produces an unambiguous answer, and ideally a SQL query someone could run by hand against the raw tables to confirm it. "Active means currently engaged" is not implementable. "Active means subscription_status is not 'canceled', AND the member has not been in a 'paused' state for more than 30 consecutive days, AND is deduplicated to one row per person regardless of how many studio locations they hold a membership at" is implementable — and just as importantly, it's arguable, which is exactly what you want in this meeting rather than three weeks into the dbt build.

The other discipline here is writing the definition so it survives contact with real edge cases that didn't come up in the first meeting: what about a member mid-way through canceling who still has five days left in a paid period, what about someone who paused on the 29th of a 30-day grace window, what about a free trial member who never became a paying subscriber. You don't need to resolve every edge case alone — you need to surface them now, with the three team leads in the room, so the eventual intermediate dbt model (built several lessons from now) has a complete, agreed-upon spec to implement against instead of a vague mandate that gets re-litigated every time a confusing row shows up in production.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Pull every testable claim out of the Lesson 1 audit

```
FROM THE AUDIT:
  - Canceled subscriptions should not count (all three teams agree)
  - Paused subscriptions: Finance says active, Marketing says not --
    needs a rule, not a vote
  - Multi-location members: currently double-counted -- confirmed bug,
    not a disagreement
  - Engagement (check-ins/app use) describes a DIFFERENT metric than
    membership status -- these got conflated and need to be separated
```

## Step 2 — Draft the candidate rule and pressure-test it live

```
DRAFT RULE v1:
"A member is ACTIVE on a given day if their subscription status is not
'canceled', they have not been continuously 'paused' for more than 30
days, and they are counted exactly once regardless of how many studio
locations their membership covers."
```

Run it past the room immediately:

```
DANA: What about someone who canceled on the 3rd but paid through
      the 30th? Are they active those last 27 days?
YOU:  Good catch -- that's a grace-period question we need a yes/no
      on, not a guess. Marcus, what does Finance's revenue recognition
      already assume?
MARCUS: We recognize revenue through the paid period, even after
        cancellation is submitted. So yes, active through the paid
        period end date.
PRIYA: Then I want that written down, because my 30-day engagement
       number isn't the same metric as this at all -- can we just
       rename mine to "Engaged Member" instead of fighting over
       "Active"?
YOU:  Yes -- that's actually the cleanest fix in this whole meeting.
```

That exchange just split one contested metric into two correctly-named ones — a real resolution, not a compromise that satisfies nobody.

## Step 3 — Write the rule with a verification query attached

```
ACTIVE MEMBER (v1, finance-and-membership basis):
  Rule: subscription_status != 'canceled'
        AND (paused_since IS NULL OR paused_since > CURRENT_DATE - 30)
        AND paid_through_date >= reporting_date
        Deduplicated to one row per member_id, regardless of location count.

  Verification query (to run by hand against 3 sample dates during review):
    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT m.member_id)
    FROM dbo.memberships m
    WHERE m.subscription_status <> 'canceled'
      AND (m.paused_since IS NULL
           OR m.paused_since > DATEADD(day, -30, @reporting_date))
      AND m.paid_through_date >= @reporting_date;

ENGAGED MEMBER (v1, separate metric, Marketing's original intent):
  Rule: Active member (above) who also has at least one check-in or
        app session in the trailing 30 days.
```

## Step 4 — Review line by line with all three leads, get an explicit yes

Don't send this by email and treat silence as agreement. Read each clause aloud to Marcus, Priya, and Jordan individually and ask "does this match what you need, yes or no?" Jordan's answer here matters most, since the deduplication clause directly overturns Product's current (buggy) behavior — get his explicit sign-off that counting once per person, not once per location, is correct going forward.

## Step 5 — Version and date the definition

Save it as `Brightleaf_Active_Member_Definition_v1.md` with the approval date and all three names attached. This is the document Lesson 3 uses to scope what ships first, and the document the eventual dbt singular test is written directly against.

## Step 6 — Pressure-test the definition against a few real-looking rows before the meeting ends

Walk through a handful of concrete example rows together, out loud, so everyone confirms the rule produces the answer they'd expect before it's finalized:

```
EXAMPLE A: subscription_status = 'active', paused_since = NULL,
           paid_through_date = next month -> ACTIVE. Agreed by all three.

EXAMPLE B: subscription_status = 'paused', paused_since = 12 days ago,
           paid_through_date = next month -> ACTIVE (paused under 30
           days). Marcus and Dana both confirm this matches intent.

EXAMPLE C: subscription_status = 'canceled', paid_through_date = 9 days
           from now -> ACTIVE until paid_through_date passes, per
           Marcus's revenue-recognition precedent from Step 2.

EXAMPLE D: One member_id with two member_locations rows (downtown and
           uptown) -> counts ONCE. Jordan explicitly signs off that
           this overturns Product's current dashboard behavior.
```

Running real examples past the room catches a disagreement while it's still a five-minute conversation, instead of a confusing row someone notices in production three months later.

Got explicit sign-off from Finance, Marketing, and Product leads on paper, including the multi-location dedup fix Product hadn't previously agreed was a bug.

One of the three original metrics turned out to be a different question entirely — Marketing's — so we renamed and preserved it instead of forcing it into the same number.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: Which Metrics, Which Teams, What's Deferred
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard, written line around what the first version of the semantic layer actually delivers, and logging every good idea that has to wait.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have one signed-off definition of an active member, and a second, correctly separated definition of an engaged member. That's enough to start planning the pipeline — but not enough to start building it, because "fix our metrics" quietly contains a dozen other requests that surfaced the moment three stakeholder teams sat in one room together. This video draws a hard written line around v1: which metrics ship, which teams' reports get rebuilt first, and what gets explicitly deferred rather than silently dropped.

This scope document is what you'll point back to in a later lesson when Dana, excited that the active-member number finally reconciles, asks for "just one more thing" — a churn-prediction score, a lifetime-value metric, a fourth team's custom view — that would quietly turn a tightly-scoped rebuild into an open-ended one.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're fixing a leaky roof. While you're up there, everyone in the house starts shouting out other things they'd like fixed too — the gutter, the chimney, maybe a whole new deck. Those might all be good ideas! But if you try to do all of them at once, the roof never actually gets finished, and the roof was the thing that was actually leaking right now.

So the smart move is to write two lists: "this is what we're fixing this weekend" and "this is the list for next time." Everyone's idea gets written down and nobody feels ignored, but the roof — the actual urgent problem — gets done first.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is scope management applied to a metrics-governance project specifically, and the failure mode to guard against is subtly different from a typical feature build: once stakeholders see one metric reconciled and trustworthy, their appetite expands immediately, because trust in one number creates demand for more trustworthy numbers. That's a good problem to have, but it still has to be managed with the same discipline as any other scope boundary — every request gets an explicit disposition (in v1, deferred to v2, or rejected), never a silent drop, because silently dropped requests resurface later as surprises and erode exactly the trust you're trying to build.

For Brightleaf specifically, the v1 boundary needs to separate "what does the governed semantic layer need to get right structurally" from "what's a nice analytical extension built on top of it later." The active-member and engaged-member definitions, plus a revenue metric Finance needs reconciled against the same membership logic, are structural — get these wrong and everything built afterward inherits the error. A churn-prediction model, a marketing-attribution view, or a lifetime-value calculation are valuable, but they're analytical layers that should be built on top of a already-trustworthy foundation, not rushed into v1 alongside it. Naming that distinction explicitly is what lets you say yes to good ideas without letting them derail the one thing that actually has to ship first.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — List everything that came up across the first two meetings that isn't in the v1 definition

```
MENTIONED, NOT YET SCOPED:
  - Revenue reconciled to the same membership basis (Finance)
  - A churn-risk score per member (Dana, mentioned twice)
  - Marketing campaign attribution tied to engagement (Priya)
  - Lifetime value per member (Dana)
  - A fourth team (Studio Operations) wants staffing-vs-attendance view
  - Historical backfill of the corrected definition for trend reporting
```

## Step 2 — Give each item an explicit, honest disposition

```
ITEM                                DISPOSITION      WHY
Revenue reconciled to membership    Included in v1   Same root cause as
  basis                                                the active-member
                                                       problem; Finance's
                                                       trust depends on it.
Churn-risk score                    Deferred to v2    Needs a modeling
                                                       effort of its own,
                                                       built on top of a
                                                       trustworthy member
                                                       history -- which v1
                                                       doesn't have yet.
Marketing attribution               Deferred to v2    Depends on a
                                                       campaign-tracking
                                                       source not yet
                                                       connected to this
                                                       pipeline at all.
Lifetime value                      Deferred to v2    Same reason as
                                                       churn-risk -- a
                                                       derived metric, not
                                                       a foundation.
Studio Operations staffing view     Rejected (for now) Different team,
                                                       different source
                                                       data, no discovery
                                                       done yet -- needs
                                                       its own kickoff.
Historical backfill of corrected    Included in v1    Needed so month-
  definition                                            over-month trends
                                                       don't break the day
                                                       the new number ships.
```

## Step 3 — Write the v1 scope statement plainly

```
BRIGHTLEAF SEMANTIC LAYER -- V1 SCOPE

Ships in v1:
  - One governed Active Member metric (per Lesson 2 definition)
  - One governed Engaged Member metric
  - Revenue reconciled against the same membership basis
  - Historical backfill so trends don't break at cutover
  - Rebuilt Power BI reports for Finance, Marketing, and Product,
    all reading from the same underlying marts

Explicitly deferred to v2 (not forgotten, logged):
  - Churn-risk scoring
  - Marketing campaign attribution
  - Lifetime value calculation
  - Studio Operations staffing/attendance view (needs its own discovery)
```

## Step 4 — Rehearse the scope-creep conversation before it happens mid-build

```
DANA: Since we're already rebuilding all this, can we just add the
      churn score too? It feels related.
YOU:  It is related, and it's already first on the v2 list. Adding it
      now means building a model on top of a foundation that hasn't
      been tested and proven yet -- we'd be guessing at churn using
      data we haven't finished validating. I'd rather ship the trusted
      foundation first, then build churn on top of something solid in
      a few weeks, than rush both and have you doubt the churn score
      the same way you doubt today's numbers.
```

That answer isn't a no — it hands Dana the real tradeoff and protects the foundation the whole rest of the series depends on.

## Step 5 — Get written sign-off on the boundary

Attach this scope statement to the Lesson 2 definition document and ask Dana for one explicit confirmation covering both. This pairing — the definition plus the boundary — is what you reopen near the end of this series when the finished platform ships and the v2 conversation formally starts.

## Step 6 — Name which team's report gets rebuilt in which order

Scope isn't only which metrics ship — it's also the sequence the three teams' reports get touched in, since all three can't be rebuilt simultaneously with one analytics engineer:

```
REBUILD ORDER FOR V1:
  1. Finance's report first -- revenue reconciliation is the most
     board-visible number, and Marcus's team has the clearest existing
     definition to migrate off of.
  2. Marketing's report second -- once Engaged Member exists as its
     own governed metric, Priya's campaign targeting can move onto it
     without waiting on anything further.
  3. Product's report last -- it requires the deduplication fix, which
     depends on the same intermediate logic Finance and Marketing's
     reports will have already validated by then.
```

Share this order with all three leads now, so nobody is surprised mid-project that their report isn't first — and so each team can see their own place on a concrete, dated plan rather than an open-ended promise.

Churn scoring, attribution, and lifetime value are explicitly deferred — they're derived metrics that need to sit on top of a validated foundation, not ship alongside it. Logged all of it so nothing gets "forgotten" and re-litigated mid-build.

That gives us a fast, non-confrontational answer the moment a new request shows up mid-build instead of letting it quietly expand the timeline.
