That protects this phase's delivery date without losing a single idea the client raised.

lessons.title: Choosing the Stack: Why Snowflake + dbt, Not Just More SQL Server Views
lessons.summary: The first architecture decision: why a Snowflake-plus-dbt layer solves a problem that writing one more SQL Server view cannot.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: With v1 scoped, this is the first real architecture decision: what actually gets built. The tempting, cheapest-looking answer is the one Brightleaf has effectively tried three times already — write one more SQL Server view with the "correct" active-member logic in it, point everyone at that view, and call it done. This video explains in detail why that approach is the root cause of the original problem, not a fix for it, and why the right answer instead is a new layer entirely: a Snowflake warehouse fed by a nightly extraction, with a version-controlled, tested dbt project sitting on top of it, which is what the rest of this series builds piece by piece.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine three kids keep arguing about how tall a plant is because each of them measures it with a different ruler kept in their own room. One fix would be to buy one really nice new ruler and put it in one kid's room — but the other two kids will probably just keep using their own rulers anyway, out of habit, or because they can't easily get to that room.

The better fix is to put one official ruler, with its measurement written down and dated, somewhere all three kids walk past every single day, and to make a rule that nobody is allowed to just make up their own number anymore — they have to use the one on the wall. That shared, visible, written-down ruler is basically what Snowflake and dbt give Brightleaf: one place everyone actually uses, instead of one more private view that only fixes the problem for whoever remembers to use it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A single corrected SQL Server view would technically solve the logic problem for about as long as it takes someone to write a new ad-hoc query against the base tables instead — which is exactly the failure mode that produced three definitions in the first place. The deeper issue at Brightleaf isn't that nobody has ever written correct SQL; Finance's, Marketing's, and Product's queries are each internally reasonable. The issue is governance: there has never been a single, discoverable, change-controlled, tested source of truth that three independent teams are structurally incentivized to actually use instead of writing their own.

That's why the right fix is a new layer, not a better query in the old one. SQL Server stays exactly as it is — untouched, read-only, the system of record it has always been — because re-architecting a live transactional database that the studio check-in and billing systems depend on is out of scope and unnecessarily risky. A nightly extraction (built in Python, orchestrated by Airflow) copies raw data out into Snowflake, a platform built for exactly this kind of analytical workload and decoupled entirely from the operational system. On top of that raw landing zone, dbt provides the three things a lone SQL Server view structurally cannot: version control through Git, so every change to the active-member logic has an author, a date, and a reviewable diff instead of living silently inside a view definition; automated tests, so a broken definition fails a pull request instead of shipping to production; and documentation and lineage that make the logic discoverable by name, so a new analyst joining any of the three teams finds the governed model before they'd ever think to write their own query against raw tables. None of this requires replacing anything Brightleaf already owns and trusts on the transactional side — it requires adding a layer specifically built for the problem that kept recurring.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — List the actual constraints before naming a single tool

```
CONSTRAINTS:
  - SQL Server is the system of record for billing and check-ins and
    must stay read-only and untouched -- no new load-bearing logic
    added directly to the operational database
  - Three teams, each with their own BI tool access today, need to
    query ONE shared source going forward, not a view only one team
    remembers to use
  - The root cause was ungoverned logic with no change history --
    whatever we choose has to make a definition change visible,
    reviewable, and testable, not just "correct right now"
  - Reporting is daily/trend-based, not real-time -- a nightly batch
    is sufficient, which rules out needing streaming infrastructure
```

## Step 2 — Assign one layer per responsibility

```
LAYER                TOOL        RESPONSIBLE FOR              NOT RESPONSIBLE FOR
Source of record      SQL Server  Durable operational storage;  Shared analytical
                                   billing and check-in systems  logic, testing,
                                   of record                     version control
Extraction/orchestr.  Python +    Nightly, scheduled, logged     Transformation
                      Airflow     copy of raw tables into        logic, business
                                   Snowflake                      rules
Analytical storage/   Snowflake   Decoupled compute and          Defining what
  compute                         storage for everything          "active" means
                                   downstream of extraction
Governed business      dbt         Staging/intermediate/mart      Raw storage,
  logic + tests                    layers; the ONE active-member  orchestration,
                                   definition; automated tests    scheduling
Version control/CI     Git +       Every change to the            Running the
                       GitHub      definition reviewed and        warehouse itself
                                   tested before it can merge
Consumption            Power BI    What Finance, Marketing, and   Defining the
                                   Product actually query          metric itself
```

## Step 3 — Name the alternative seriously considered, and why it loses

```
- One more corrected SQL Server view: rejected. This is literally
  what produced the original problem -- logic with no version
  history, no test, and no structural reason three teams would all
  discover and use the same one going forward.
- Rebuilding reports directly against raw SQL Server tables from
  Power BI, no transformation layer: rejected. Puts the business
  logic back inside DAX measures per-report, which is the same
  governance failure in a different tool.
- Doing the transformation work as stored procedures inside SQL
  Server instead of dbt: considered, but rejected for this project --
  stored procedures have no built-in test framework, no documentation
  generation, and mixing heavy analytical transformation workload
  onto the live operational database risks the billing system's
  performance, which the business cannot accept.
```

## Step 4 — Write the one-paragraph justification you'll reuse later

```
"We're keeping SQL Server exactly as it is -- it's not broken, it's
ungoverned downstream of it. We're adding a nightly extraction into
Snowflake and a tested, version-controlled dbt project on top of it,
so the active-member definition lives in exactly one place, changes
to it go through review, and every team's Power BI report reads from
the same governed mart instead of writing its own query again."
```

## Step 5 — Write down what this choice does NOT require, since that's often the real objection

```
THIS DECISION DOES NOT REQUIRE:
  - Migrating the billing or check-in systems off SQL Server
  - Any downtime or risk to the live operational database
  - Retraining store staff or changing anything members experience
  - A cloud migration beyond the analytical workload itself --
    Snowflake holds a COPY of the data, extracted nightly, not the
    operational system of record
```

Saying plainly what this architecture does *not* touch is often what actually gets a cautious stakeholder to approve it — the fear behind "do we really need a new platform" is almost always about risk to the systems that already work, not about cost, and naming the boundary directly addresses that fear instead of leaving it unspoken.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the architecture: SQL Server stays untouched as the system of record, a nightly Python extraction orchestrated by Airflow lands raw data into Snowflake, and dbt owns every layer of transformation and business logic from there, with Git and CI enforcing that no definition change ships without a passing test. Rejected a one-more-view fix explicitly, since that's the exact pattern that produced three conflicting numbers in the first place.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We're not touching the system that already runs billing and check-ins — we're adding a new, properly governed layer on top of it so all three teams end up reading from the same place. This also means future changes to the definition go through a reviewable process instead of living inside someone's personal SQL query.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We're not ripping out or risking the system that runs your billing today. We're adding a new layer specifically built so Finance, Marketing, and Product all read the same number going forward, with every future change to that number tracked and reviewed instead of buried in someone's private report.

lessons.title: Designing the dbt Layering: Staging, Intermediate, Marts
lessons.summary: Whiteboarding dbt's staging, intermediate, and marts layers — and where the one true "active member" definition will live — before writing a single model.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With Snowflake and dbt chosen as the stack, this is the first real architecture decision inside dbt itself: how the project's models are layered. We're whiteboarding three layers — **staging** (one model per raw source table, light cleanup only), **intermediate** (where the actual business logic lives, most importantly the single model that will define "active member" for all of Brightleaf Fitness), and **marts** (the wide, final tables Power BI and every team will actually query) — before opening an editor and writing a line of SQL.

This layering decision is the architectural core of the entire series. Every later lesson — the staging models in the implementation phase, the active-member logic, the two marts, even the fanout bug this project eventually hits and fixes — happens inside the shape drawn in this lesson. Get the boundary between "cleanup" and "business logic" wrong here, and the project ends up right back where it started: three teams with three different, hard-to-audit definitions, just now written in dbt instead of three ad-hoc SQL scripts.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine sorting a huge pile of mixed laundry before it gets washed, dried, and put away. First you just separate it into piles — whites, darks, towels — without deciding anything complicated, just sorting. Then you make the real decisions: this shirt has a stain so it needs the stain treatment, these socks are a matched pair so they stay together. Only at the very end do you fold everything into neat stacks and put it in the right drawer, ready for someone to actually grab and wear.

dbt works the same way across three "rooms." The first room just tidies each pile a little (staging). The second room is where the real decisions get made, like "is this member actually still paying and active today, or did they pause?" (intermediate). The third room folds everything into neat, labeled stacks that Finance, Marketing, and Product can each open and trust (marts). Nobody skips straight from the messy pile to the drawer — every piece of data passes through all three rooms in order.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is dbt's standard staging to intermediate to marts layering, and the discipline that matters is keeping each layer honest about its one job. **Staging** models are 1:1 with a source table — renamed columns, cast types, trimmed strings, nothing else. No joins, no `CASE` logic deciding what counts as "active," no filtering out rows that look wrong. A staging model with business logic in it is the single most common way a dbt project quietly becomes unauditable, because now there are two places someone has to check to understand a number instead of one.

**Intermediate** models are where Brightleaf's real problem gets solved: one model, `int_active_members`, that encodes the business rule every team will share, handling the two edge cases that have been producing three different numbers for years — a membership on "pause" status should not count as active even though the parent membership row says active, and a member holding memberships at two locations at once must be counted once, not twice. **Marts** are wide, denormalized, and built for consumption — `member_activity_mart` and `revenue_mart` are the only models Power BI's semantic model (built later in this series) is allowed to query directly. That last rule is itself a governance decision: if a report ever needs to reach past the marts into intermediate or staging, that's a sign the marts are missing something, not a reason to let the report reach backward.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Write the one sentence this whole project exists to produce

Before naming a single model, write down the actual business rule in plain language, the same way a star-schema project writes a grain statement before touching a table:

```
ACTIVE MEMBER (as of a given day) =
  a member with at least one membership row whose status is 'active'
  on that day, MINUS any day covered by an approved pause,
  counted ONCE even if they hold active memberships at more than
  one Brightleaf location at the same time.
```

Every model built from here forward gets checked against this sentence. If a model's logic can't trace back to a clause in it, that logic doesn't belong in this project yet.

## Step 2 — Assign each layer exactly one job, and write down what each is NOT allowed to do

```
LAYER         JOB                                    NOT ALLOWED TO DO
staging       1:1 cleanup of one source table:        Joins, business logic,
              rename, cast, trim, standardize          filtering "bad" rows,
              casing/nulls                              deciding what's "active"
intermediate  The real business logic: status          Being queried directly
              history, pause handling, dedup            by Power BI
marts         Wide, join-ready, final answer            Any NEW logic --
              tables -- the only thing                   marts assemble,
              Power BI is allowed to query                they don't decide
```

## Step 3 — Map the real source tables to staging models

Brightleaf's nightly extraction lands six raw tables in Snowflake: `MEMBERS`, `MEMBERSHIPS`, `MEMBERSHIP_STATUS_HISTORY`, `LOCATIONS`, `PAYMENTS`, `STUDIO_CHECKINS`. Each gets exactly one staging model, named `stg_brightleaf__<table>`:

```sql
-- models/staging/brightleaf/stg_brightleaf__memberships.sql
with source as (
    select * from {{ source('brightleaf', 'memberships') }}
),
renamed as (
    select
        membership_id::varchar            as membership_id,
        member_id::varchar                as member_id,
        location_id::varchar              as home_location_id,
        plan_code::varchar                as plan_code,
        start_date::date                  as membership_start_date,
        end_date::date                    as membership_end_date,
        lower(trim(status))::varchar      as membership_status,
        _loaded_at                        as _staging_loaded_at
    from source
)
select * from renamed
```

Notice what's missing on purpose: no filter on `membership_status`, no join to `membership_status_history`. That logic belongs one layer up.

## Step 4 — Whiteboard the one intermediate model that matters most

`int_active_members` is where the pause and multi-location edge cases actually get resolved, by turning the status history into dated intervals and collapsing anyone active at two locations into one row per member per day:

```sql
-- models/intermediate/int_active_members.sql
with status_spine as (
    select
        member_id,
        membership_id,
        membership_status,
        effective_date,
        lead(effective_date) over (
            partition by membership_id order by effective_date
        ) as next_effective_date
    from {{ ref('stg_brightleaf__membership_status_history') }}
),
active_intervals as (
    select
        member_id,
        membership_id,
        effective_date as status_start_date,
        coalesce(next_effective_date, current_date()) as status_end_date
    from status_spine
    where membership_status = 'active'   -- excludes 'paused' explicitly
)
-- a member can be active at two locations at once; this collapses
-- that to one row per member per day so member_activity_mart never
-- double-counts them
select distinct member_id, status_start_date, status_end_date
from active_intervals
```

## Step 5 — Whiteboard the two marts, and lock what each is for

```
member_activity_mart  -- one row per member per day: is_active flag,
                         home_location, plan_code. What Marketing and
                         Product query for "how many active members."
revenue_mart          -- joins payments to active status. What Finance
                         queries for "revenue per active member."
```

## Step 6 — Lay out the folder structure and materializations before writing anything else

```
models/
  staging/brightleaf/
    _brightleaf__sources.yml
    stg_brightleaf__members.sql
    stg_brightleaf__memberships.sql
    stg_brightleaf__membership_status_history.sql
    stg_brightleaf__locations.sql
    stg_brightleaf__payments.sql
    stg_brightleaf__studio_checkins.sql
  intermediate/
    int_active_members.sql
  marts/
    member_activity_mart.sql
    revenue_mart.sql
```

```yaml
# dbt_project.yml
models:
  brightleaf_analytics:
    staging:
      +materialized: view
    intermediate:
      +materialized: view
    marts:
      +materialized: table
```

Views for staging and intermediate keep the project cheap to iterate on; marts materialize as tables because Power BI queries them directly and needs them fast and stable.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Whiteboarded the dbt layering before writing a model: staging stays strictly 1:1 with the six raw source tables, the active-member business rule — including pause handling and multi-location dedup — lives in exactly one intermediate model, and Power BI is only ever allowed to query the two marts. That boundary is what keeps this from turning into three ad-hoc definitions again, just inside dbt.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've mapped out how the data will flow through dbt before any code gets written — raw tables, one shared business-logic layer, then two final tables each team queries. This is the step that guarantees Finance, Marketing, and Product end up looking at the same number, not three different ones built in the same tool.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We designed exactly how the member data gets cleaned, defined, and finalized — with one single, written rule for what counts as an active member — before building anything. That's the structural fix for the number-disagreement problem, not just a patch on top of it.

lessons.title: Planning the Git Workflow and CI Checks Before Writing a Model
lessons.summary: Deciding the branch, pull-request, and CI rules that keep a broken model or failing test out of main before any dbt code exists.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The dbt layering from Lesson 5 defines what gets built. This lesson plans the process around *how* it gets built and shipped safely — the Git branching convention, the pull-request rule, and the continuous-integration check that runs `dbt build` and `dbt test` on every proposed change — before a single model file exists in the repository. For a project whose entire purpose is restoring trust in a number, the mechanism that prevents a broken or untested model from reaching `main` is not a nice-to-have; it's the same kind of load-bearing decision as the active-member definition itself.

This is also the plan that makes the rest of the series safe to build incrementally. Staging models, the intermediate active-member logic, the marts, and the eventual fanout-bug fix all land through this same branch, pull request, CI, merge path — so getting the rule right here means every later lesson in the series inherits a safety net instead of needing to invent one under pressure.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a shared class notebook where everyone's grade depends on it staying accurate. You wouldn't let just anyone scribble directly in the one official copy — instead, you'd write your changes on a separate sheet first, have a friend check it over, and only copy it into the official notebook once someone confirms it's correct. That way a mistake gets caught on the scratch sheet, never in the notebook everyone relies on.

That's exactly the rule we're setting up for this project's code. Nobody edits the "official" version directly. Every change starts on its own separate copy, gets reviewed, and only joins the official version after a robot checker and a person both say it's correct.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is a trunk-based Git workflow with branch protection, and the two mechanisms doing the real work are the pull request and the CI gate. `main` is always deployable and is never committed to directly — every change, from a new staging model to a one-line fix, lives on its own short-lived feature branch, named for what it does (`feature/int-active-members`, `fix/membership-fanout`), and reaches `main` only through a pull request.

The pull request itself is necessary but not sufficient — a human reviewer can miss a broken model the same way a human regional manager missed a bad SQL join for years. The CI check is what makes the guarantee real: on every pull request, GitHub Actions spins up a dbt run against a dedicated CI schema in Snowflake (never production) and runs `dbt build` followed by `dbt test` — the standard tests (`unique`, `not_null`, `accepted_values`) plus the custom singular test asserting the active-member rule holds. Branch protection on `main` then makes passing that check a precondition of merging, not a courtesy — a model that fails a test literally cannot reach the marts Power BI reads from. That's the mechanical reason a broken `int_active_members` model can be caught in a pull request instead of showing up as a wrong number in next month's board deck.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Decide the branching rule before any code exists

```
main                                -- always deployable, never committed
                                       to directly
feature/<short-description>         -- one branch per model or ticket
fix/<short-description>             -- one branch per bug fix

Examples:
  feature/stg-brightleaf-sources
  feature/int-active-members
  feature/add-revenue-mart
  fix/membership-fanout
```

Every branch name should tell a reviewer what it changes without opening it — that habit pays off directly later in this series, when `git log` needs to answer "which change introduced this."

## Step 2 — Decide what a pull request must contain before it can be reviewed

```
PULL REQUEST CHECKLIST
  [ ] Ran `dbt build` locally against a personal dev schema
  [ ] Added or updated schema.yml tests for any new/changed column
  [ ] If this changes a model another model or exposure depends on,
      that dependency is called out in the PR description
  [ ] No hard-coded warehouse-specific values (Snowflake account,
      database names) outside dbt_project.yml / profiles
```

This checklist is a lightweight PR template committed to the repo at `.github/pull_request_template.md` so it shows up automatically every time.

## Step 3 — Write the actual CI workflow

```yaml
# .github/workflows/dbt_ci.yml
name: dbt CI

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  dbt_build_and_test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT }}
      SNOWFLAKE_USER: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_CI_USER }}
      SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_CI_PASSWORD }}
      SNOWFLAKE_ROLE: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_CI_ROLE }}
      SNOWFLAKE_WAREHOUSE: CI_WH
      SNOWFLAKE_DATABASE: BRIGHTLEAF_CI
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - run: pip install dbt-snowflake
      - run: dbt deps
      - run: dbt build
      - run: dbt test
```

Every secret is a CI-specific credential scoped to a `BRIGHTLEAF_CI` database — the check never touches production, so a pull request can run `dbt build` as many times as needed without any risk to the real marts.

## Step 4 — Turn the CI check into a hard gate with branch protection

```
BRANCH PROTECTION RULE on main:
  - Require a pull request before merging
  - Require at least 1 approving review
  - Require the "dbt_build_and_test" status check to pass
  - Disallow force-pushes to main
  - Disallow direct commits to main (including by admins)
```

With this rule in place, a model with a failing `unique` test or a singular test asserting the active-member rule simply cannot be merged — the merge button stays disabled until CI reports green.

## Step 5 — Add a CODEOWNERS rule for the marts folder specifically

```
# .github/CODEOWNERS
# Any change under models/marts/ requires sign-off from the
# analytics engineering lead, since these are the only models
# the three business teams query directly.
/models/marts/  @brightleaf-analytics-lead
```

Staging and intermediate changes only need the standard one-reviewer rule from Step 4. Marts get an extra layer of review because a change here — even a seemingly small one, like adding a column — is the one most likely to be visible to Finance, Marketing, or Product the very next morning.

## Step 6 — Write down what CI does NOT replace

```
CI catches: broken SQL, failing schema tests, a singular test failure.
CI does NOT catch: "is this the right business logic," "did we agree
this is what 'active' should mean." That's still a human review
question, which is why the pull-request review step stays mandatory
even though CI is automated.
```

This distinction matters later in the series: when the active-member count still doesn't match Finance's after everything is green, the bug isn't a failed test — it's a correct-looking model doing the wrong thing, which only a careful review or a deliberate investigation catches.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the Git workflow before writing a model: short-lived feature branches, mandatory pull requests, and a GitHub Actions check that runs dbt build and dbt test against a dedicated CI schema on every PR. Branch protection on main makes that check a hard gate, not a suggestion — nothing merges without it passing and a human review.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've set up the process that keeps a mistake from ever reaching the live reports: every change gets reviewed and automatically tested before it's allowed into the main codebase. That's what lets us build the rest of this project in small, safe steps instead of one risky big-bang release.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Before writing the business logic, we put a safety check in place so a broken change can't quietly reach your dashboards — every update to the data pipeline gets automatically tested and reviewed first. This is the same kind of control serious engineering teams run on production software.

lessons.title: Planning the Ingestion Path: SQL Server to Snowflake
lessons.summary: Mapping the nightly Python extraction, Airflow orchestration, and batch window that lands SQL Server data in Snowflake before dbt ever runs.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The dbt layers and the Git/CI workflow are both planned, but neither one has anything to run against yet — Snowflake is still empty. This lesson plans how data actually gets from Brightleaf's legacy on-premises SQL Server into Snowflake every night: which tables get a full nightly snapshot versus an incremental load, what a nightly Python extraction script actually does, and how Airflow orchestrates and schedules the whole thing — all worked out on paper, backward from the time Finance, Marketing, and Product need fresh numbers, before writing a line of Python.

This is also the last architecture-planning lesson before implementation starts. Every decision here — table-by-table extraction strategy, the DAG shape, the schedule — becomes the literal Airflow DAG and Python script built later in the series, the same way a planning lesson in any real BI project becomes the actual pipeline a few lessons later.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a delivery truck that has to move boxes every single night from an old, cluttered warehouse across town into a brand-new, organized one — and the new warehouse has to be fully stocked and ready before the store opens in the morning. You wouldn't just start driving randomly; you'd plan the route backward from opening time: when does the old warehouse finish packing boxes, how long does the drive take, how much extra time should you leave in case of traffic?

That's exactly the planning happening here, just with data instead of boxes. Every night, information has to move from Brightleaf's old computer system into the new one, and it all has to be ready well before anyone at the company checks their numbers in the morning.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is ingestion planning: deciding, per source table, whether a nightly load should be a full snapshot or an incremental pull, then wrapping that decision in an orchestrator with real scheduling and failure semantics. Brightleaf's six source tables don't all behave the same way, so they don't all get the same strategy — `members` and `locations` are small and slow-changing, so a full nightly snapshot is simpler and cheap; `memberships`, `membership_status_history`, `payments`, and `studio_checkins` are large and append-heavy, so each gets an incremental pull keyed on a watermark column (`updated_at` or a timestamp) tracked in a small watermark table, so the nightly job only pulls what actually changed.

The mechanism is a Python extraction script per table — querying SQL Server over `pyodbc`, writing Parquet files to a Snowflake internal stage, then `COPY INTO` landing the raw tables — orchestrated by one Airflow DAG with one task per table running in parallel, followed by a task that triggers the dbt job once every extraction has succeeded. Scheduling works backward from the deadline, the same discipline as any nightly-batch BI project: Brightleaf's SQL Server batch closes out by 11pm, so the DAG is scheduled for 1:00am with a comfortable buffer already built in, targeting full completion — extraction, load, and a successful `dbt build`/`dbt test` — hours before the 7am point at which any of the three teams might open a dashboard.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Decide an extraction strategy per table, not one strategy for everything

```
TABLE                       SIZE/CHANGE PATTERN        STRATEGY
members                     Small, slow-changing        Full nightly snapshot
locations                   Tiny (~40 rows), rarely      Full nightly snapshot
                             changes
memberships                 Medium, changes often        Incremental on
                                                          updated_at watermark
membership_status_history   Append-only, grows daily     Incremental on
                                                          effective_date
payments                    Large, append-heavy          Incremental on
                                                          payment_date watermark
studio_checkins              Largest, highest volume      Incremental on
                                                          checkin_timestamp
```

A full snapshot every night is simpler to reason about and cheap for a 40-row table; running that same strategy against millions of check-in rows would make the nightly job slow for no benefit, which is why the split matters.

## Step 2 — Plan the extraction mechanics, per table

```
1. Python script reads the table's watermark table (or does a full pull
   for snapshot tables) and queries SQL Server via pyodbc for new/changed
   rows.
2. Writes the result to Parquet, locally or directly to a Snowflake
   internal stage via PUT.
3. Runs COPY INTO against the matching raw landing table in Snowflake.
4. Updates the watermark table with the new high-water mark on success
   only -- a failed run leaves the watermark untouched so a retry
   re-pulls the same window instead of skipping it.
```

## Step 3 — Plan the Airflow DAG shape

```python
# dags/brightleaf_sql_server_to_snowflake.py
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

default_args = {
    "retries": 2,
    "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=10),
    "on_failure_callback": alert_slack_data_platform,
}

with DAG(
    dag_id="brightleaf_sql_server_to_snowflake",
    schedule_interval="0 1 * * *",     # 1:00am daily
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
    catchup=False,
    default_args=default_args,
    sla_miss_callback=alert_slack_data_platform,
) as dag:

    extract_members = PythonOperator(
        task_id="extract_members",
        python_callable=extract_and_load,
        op_kwargs={"table": "members", "strategy": "full_snapshot"},
    )
    extract_memberships = PythonOperator(
        task_id="extract_memberships",
        python_callable=extract_and_load,
        op_kwargs={"table": "memberships", "strategy": "incremental",
                   "watermark_col": "updated_at"},
    )
    extract_checkins = PythonOperator(
        task_id="extract_studio_checkins",
        python_callable=extract_and_load,
        op_kwargs={"table": "studio_checkins", "strategy": "incremental",
                   "watermark_col": "checkin_timestamp"},
    )
    trigger_dbt_run = PythonOperator(
        task_id="trigger_dbt_run",
        python_callable=trigger_dbt_cloud_job,
    )

    [extract_members, extract_memberships, extract_checkins] >> trigger_dbt_run
```

Extraction tasks run in parallel since the tables don't depend on each other; `dbt` only runs once every extraction has succeeded, since the staging models read from all six raw tables.

## Step 4 — Build the actual backward-planned schedule

```
11:00pm -- SQL Server's nightly batch close finishes; source data for
           the day is final
 1:00am -- Airflow DAG starts (2-hour buffer already built in past
           batch close)
 2:15am -- All six tables extracted and landed as raw Snowflake tables
 2:30am -- dbt build + dbt test triggered against production schemas
 3:15am -- member_activity_mart and revenue_mart refreshed
 7:00am -- Earliest any of Finance/Marketing/Product opens a dashboard
           -- nearly four hours of slack beyond the pipeline's expected
           finish time
```

## Step 5 — Decide failure handling before it's needed

```
- Each extraction task retries twice, 10 minutes apart, before failing
  the DAG run.
- Incremental loads are watermark-safe: a failed run doesn't advance
  the watermark, so a retry re-pulls the same window rather than
  silently skipping rows.
- Any task failure or SLA miss posts to the #data-platform-alerts
  Slack channel -- a shared channel, not one person's inbox.
- trigger_dbt_run only fires if ALL extraction tasks succeeded --
  dbt never builds on top of a partially-landed night.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned the ingestion path before writing any Python: small reference tables get a full nightly snapshot, high-volume tables load incrementally off a watermark column, and one Airflow DAG orchestrates all six extractions in parallel before triggering dbt. Scheduled for 1am, which leaves close to four hours of buffer ahead of anyone opening a dashboard at 7am.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've mapped out exactly how data gets from the old SQL Server system into Snowflake every night, including what happens if a piece fails partway through. That means the pipeline has real breathing room before the business day starts, instead of racing the clock.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The nightly handoff from the legacy system into the new platform is fully planned, with hours of safety margin built in before anyone at the company looks at the numbers. That buffer is exactly what prevents a slow or failed night from becoming your problem.

lessons.title: Standing Up the Snowflake Warehouse and Loading Raw Data
lessons.summary: Opening Snowflake for the first time to create the warehouse, database, and raw landing tables, then proving the load path with a real COPY INTO.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Planning is done — this is the first lesson where the Snowflake UI actually opens. We're standing up `BRIGHTLEAF_WH` (the virtual warehouse that does the compute), `BRIGHTLEAF_RAW` (the database where each night's extraction lands, exactly as it arrives from SQL Server), and the raw landing tables for all six source tables planned in Lesson 7 — then proving the whole load path works with a real `COPY INTO` before Airflow is ever asked to run it on a schedule.

Nothing built in this lesson is governed, cleaned, or business-ready yet, and that's deliberate. `BRIGHTLEAF_RAW` is a landing zone, not the dbt "staging" layer whiteboarded in Lesson 5 — those are two different things that happen to share a similar idea: this raw database holds whatever the nightly extraction actually produced, untyped and unfiltered, so dbt's own staging models (built next in this series) have something honest to clean up, rather than a database that's already quietly made assumptions for them.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture building a brand-new warehouse building before any boxes ever arrive. First you put up the building and turn on the lights and loading dock (the Snowflake warehouse). Then you label the shelves for exactly the kinds of boxes that are coming (the raw tables). Only after all of that do you actually drive the first truck up and unload boxes onto those shelves, then count them to make sure nothing fell off the truck.

That's exactly what happens in this lesson — except the "boxes" are rows of membership and payment data, and we're building the very first version of the warehouse they'll land in every single night from now on.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Snowflake's compute (the virtual warehouse) and storage (databases/schemas/tables) are billed and scaled independently, which is the first real decision here: an `XSMALL`, auto-suspending warehouse is more than enough for one nightly batch load of this size, and `AUTO_SUSPEND`/`AUTO_RESUME` keep it from burning credits sitting idle between runs. The second decision is schema permissiveness, for the same reason a well-built staging layer anywhere lands wide, loosely-typed columns: raw landing tables use `VARCHAR` for nearly everything, plus load-metadata columns (`_source_file_name`, `_loaded_at`) that don't exist in the source system at all, so that a malformed value from SQL Server lands successfully and gets caught deliberately in dbt's staging layer, instead of silently failing a typed `COPY INTO` at 1am with nobody watching.

The third decision is the one worth being precise about out loud, because the vocabulary genuinely overlaps: `BRIGHTLEAF_RAW` is a Snowflake database — a landing zone for whatever the Python extraction produced, with no relationship to dbt's model layers. The dbt "staging" layer from Lesson 5 (the `stg_brightleaf__*` models) is a transformation layer that reads *from* this raw database and writes its output into a separate analytics database. They share a word because they share a philosophy — land first, clean second — but conflating the Snowflake database with the dbt layer is a common point of confusion on real projects, and worth naming plainly before it causes one here.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Create the virtual warehouse and the raw database

```sql
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS BRIGHTLEAF_WH
  WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL'
  AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
  AUTO_RESUME = TRUE
  INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE;

CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS BRIGHTLEAF_RAW;

USE DATABASE BRIGHTLEAF_RAW;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING;
```

An `XSMALL` warehouse that auto-suspends after 60 seconds idle is the right size for a nightly batch job touching a few million rows at most — right-sizing this now avoids paying for idle compute between nightly runs.

## Step 2 — Create a file format and internal stage for the nightly extraction

```sql
CREATE FILE FORMAT IF NOT EXISTS BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING.PARQUET_FORMAT
  TYPE = PARQUET;

CREATE STAGE IF NOT EXISTS BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING.NIGHTLY_EXTRACT_STAGE
  FILE_FORMAT = BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING.PARQUET_FORMAT;
```

This is the stage the Python extraction script from Lesson 7 will `PUT` files into every night, organized into one subfolder per table (`/members/`, `/memberships/`, and so on).

## Step 3 — Create the raw landing tables, permissively

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING.MEMBERS (
    member_id            VARCHAR,
    first_name           VARCHAR,
    last_name            VARCHAR,
    email                VARCHAR,
    home_location_id     VARCHAR,
    signup_date          VARCHAR,
    _source_file_name    VARCHAR,
    _batch_id            VARCHAR,
    _loaded_at           TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING.MEMBERSHIPS (
    membership_id        VARCHAR,
    member_id            VARCHAR,
    location_id          VARCHAR,
    plan_code            VARCHAR,
    start_date           VARCHAR,
    end_date             VARCHAR,
    status               VARCHAR,
    updated_at           VARCHAR,
    _source_file_name    VARCHAR,
    _batch_id            VARCHAR,
    _loaded_at           TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING.MEMBERSHIP_STATUS_HISTORY (
    membership_id        VARCHAR,
    member_id            VARCHAR,
    status               VARCHAR,
    effective_date       VARCHAR,
    _source_file_name    VARCHAR,
    _batch_id            VARCHAR,
    _loaded_at           TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
);
```

Every column that comes from the source is `VARCHAR`, even obviously date-shaped ones like `start_date` — if SQL Server ever exports a malformed date, it should land successfully here and get caught deliberately in dbt's staging models, not reject the whole nightly file.

## Step 4 — Run a manual load to prove the path, before Airflow ever runs it

```sql
COPY INTO BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING.MEMBERS
FROM @BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING.NIGHTLY_EXTRACT_STAGE/members/
PATTERN = '.*\.parquet'
MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE
ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE';

COPY INTO BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING.MEMBERSHIPS
FROM @BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING.NIGHTLY_EXTRACT_STAGE/memberships/
PATTERN = '.*\.parquet'
MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE
ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE';
```

`ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE'` matches the failure philosophy planned in earlier lessons: one malformed row shouldn't block the rest of a file from loading.

## Step 5 — Confirm the load, and confirm the raw database stays untouched by dbt logic

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING.MEMBERS;
SELECT * FROM BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING.MEMBERSHIPS LIMIT 10;
```

Spot-check a few rows against the source export by hand. `BRIGHTLEAF_RAW` has no foreign keys, no typed columns beyond the metadata fields, and zero dbt models reading or writing to it directly except as a `source()` — this permissive, hands-off landing zone is exactly what makes the staging models built next in this series something you can trust the moment they run.

## Step 6 — Create a role-scoped login for the nightly load, separate from any human user

```sql
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS BRIGHTLEAF_LOADER_ROLE;
GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE BRIGHTLEAF_WH TO ROLE BRIGHTLEAF_LOADER_ROLE;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE BRIGHTLEAF_RAW TO ROLE BRIGHTLEAF_LOADER_ROLE;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING TO ROLE BRIGHTLEAF_LOADER_ROLE;
GRANT INSERT, SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA BRIGHTLEAF_RAW.LANDING
  TO ROLE BRIGHTLEAF_LOADER_ROLE;

CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS BRIGHTLEAF_AIRFLOW_SVC
  DEFAULT_ROLE = BRIGHTLEAF_LOADER_ROLE
  DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE = BRIGHTLEAF_WH;
GRANT ROLE BRIGHTLEAF_LOADER_ROLE TO USER BRIGHTLEAF_AIRFLOW_SVC;
```

The Airflow DAG from Lesson 7 authenticates as this service account, not as a personal login — it can insert and select against the raw landing tables and nothing else, which means a compromised or misconfigured credential in the nightly job can't reach the analytics database dbt builds into, let alone the marts Power BI reads from.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Stood up BRIGHTLEAF_WH and the BRIGHTLEAF_RAW database with six permissive landing tables, then proved the load path with a manual COPY INTO before handing it to Airflow. Every raw column is VARCHAR plus load metadata — typing and cleanup happen in dbt's staging models next, not here, which keeps this landing zone honest about what actually arrived each night.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Snowflake is live and the first real data has landed successfully. This is the first physical piece of infrastructure in the new platform, and it proves the nightly pipeline we planned on paper actually works end to end.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The new data platform now physically exists in Snowflake, and we've successfully loaded a first real batch of Brightleaf's data into it. This is the foundation the governed reporting layer gets built on top of over the next several steps.

lessons.title: Building the Staging Models
lessons.summary: One dbt staging model per raw Snowflake table -- light renaming and casting, no business logic yet.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Raw data is sitting in Snowflake exactly as the nightly extraction landed it: `raw.sql_server_memberships`, `raw.sql_server_billing`, and `raw.sql_server_locations`, each still carrying SQL Server's column names, text-ish types, and whatever casing the source system happened to use. This lesson builds the first real layer of the dbt project on top of them: one staging model per raw table -- `stg_memberships`, `stg_billing`, `stg_locations` -- each doing nothing but renaming columns to a consistent convention, casting them to proper types, and standardizing values like status codes. No business logic lives here at all.

That restraint is the entire point of a staging layer. Every other model in this project -- starting with the intermediate model in the next lesson -- reads from these three staging models, never from the raw tables directly. If staging already did real work, you'd have no clean place left to put the one thing every team actually disagrees about: what "active member" means.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you just got three boxes of mail from three different relatives, and each one labels things slightly differently -- one writes dates as "3/4/26," another writes "March 4 2026," a third just writes "20260304." Before you can actually use any of it, you'd want to copy everything onto matching index cards with the same date format and the same handwriting, without changing what any of it says.

That's all a staging model does. It takes the raw mail exactly as it arrived and copies it onto a tidy, consistent card -- same column names, same date format, same spelling for statuses like "active" versus "ACTIVE" versus "Active ". Nothing is decided or judged yet. That happens later, once everything already looks the same.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the staging layer in the standard dbt layering convention: staging -> intermediate -> marts. Staging models are deliberately thin -- a 1:1 relationship with a single source table, renaming and casting only, no joins, no aggregation, no filtering out rows that look wrong. The reason to keep this boundary strict is that every staging model becomes a dependency for everything built on top of it; if `stg_memberships` silently dropped rows or applied a status mapping nobody wrote down, every downstream model -- including the one that will define Brightleaf's single answer to "is this member active" -- inherits an invisible decision nobody can find later.

Each model also declares its source explicitly through dbt's `source()` function rather than hardcoding the raw table name, which is what lets `dbt docs generate` draw an accurate lineage graph back to `raw.sql_server_memberships` and what lets a future freshness check be configured against the source block without touching a single model file. We name models with a `stg_` prefix as a convention, not a requirement -- it's what makes it instantly obvious, six months from now, which models are safe to build more logic on top of (none, in this layer) versus which ones already carry governed business logic.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Declare the raw tables as dbt sources

Before writing a single staging model, declare the raw Snowflake tables in a `sources.yml` so every staging model references them through `source()` instead of a hardcoded table name:

```yaml
# models/staging/sources.yml
version: 2

sources:
  - name: sql_server_raw
    description: >
      Raw tables landed nightly into Snowflake from Brightleaf's on-prem
      SQL Server database by the Python extraction script, orchestrated
      by Airflow (see Lesson 8).
    database: brightleaf_raw
    schema: raw
    tables:
      - name: sql_server_memberships
      - name: sql_server_billing
      - name: sql_server_locations
```

## Step 2 — Build stg_memberships

`raw.sql_server_memberships` holds one row per membership *status period* -- a new row is written every time a membership's status changes, which is exactly what makes a mid-month pause visible later.

```sql
-- models/staging/stg_memberships.sql
{{ config(materialized='view') }}

with source as (

    select * from {{ source('sql_server_raw', 'sql_server_memberships') }}

)

select
    membership_status_id,
    membership_id,
    member_id,
    location_id,
    plan_code,
    upper(trim(status))                   as status,
    cast(status_start_date as date)        as status_start_date,
    cast(status_end_date as date)           as status_end_date,
    cast(monthly_rate as number(10,2))       as monthly_rate_usd,
    cast(extracted_at as timestamp_ntz)       as loaded_at
from source
```

Note what's missing: no filter dropping canceled rows, no join to locations, no decision about what counts as "active." `status_end_date` stays nullable -- a null means the period is still open today, and that nuance belongs intact in staging, not resolved here.

## Step 3 — Build stg_billing

```sql
-- models/staging/stg_billing.sql
{{ config(materialized='view') }}

with source as (

    select * from {{ source('sql_server_raw', 'sql_server_billing') }}

)

select
    billing_id,
    member_id,
    membership_id,
    cast(invoice_date as date)              as invoice_date,
    cast(billing_period_start as date)       as billing_period_start,
    cast(billing_period_end as date)          as billing_period_end,
    cast(amount_billed as number(10,2))        as amount_billed_usd,
    cast(amount_paid as number(10,2))           as amount_paid_usd,
    upper(trim(payment_status))                  as payment_status,
    cast(extracted_at as timestamp_ntz)            as loaded_at
from source
```

## Step 4 — Build stg_locations

```sql
-- models/staging/stg_locations.sql
{{ config(materialized='view') }}

with source as (

    select * from {{ source('sql_server_raw', 'sql_server_locations') }}

)

select
    location_id,
    location_name,
    city,
    state,
    region,
    cast(square_footage as integer)     as square_footage,
    cast(open_date as date)               as open_date,
    cast(is_active_location as boolean)    as is_active_location,
    cast(extracted_at as timestamp_ntz)      as loaded_at
from source
```

## Step 5 — Document and test each staging model

```yaml
# models/staging/_stg__models.yml
version: 2

models:
  - name: stg_memberships
    description: >
      One row per membership status period. Light renaming and casting
      only over raw.sql_server_memberships -- no "active member" logic
      lives here; see int_active_members.
    columns:
      - name: membership_status_id
        description: Primary key -- one row per status period.
        tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: member_id
        tests: [not_null]
      - name: status
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['ACTIVE', 'PAUSED', 'CANCELED', 'TRIAL']

  - name: stg_billing
    description: One row per invoice generated for a member.
    columns:
      - name: billing_id
        tests: [unique, not_null]

  - name: stg_locations
    description: One row per Brightleaf studio location.
    columns:
      - name: location_id
        tests: [unique, not_null]
```

## Step 6 — Run and verify

```
dbt run --select staging
dbt test --select staging
```

Check row counts against the raw tables directly (`select count(*) from raw.sql_server_memberships` versus `select count(*) from stg_memberships`) -- staging should never drop a row, so these counts must match exactly before moving on.

## Step 7 — Decide materialization deliberately, not by default

All three staging models are configured as `view`, not `table`. At this layer that's the right call: views cost nothing to keep in sync (Snowflake just re-runs the lightweight `select` against raw on every query), and since no expensive aggregation happens here, there's no performance reason to pay for storing a physical copy. That changes further down the pipeline -- `int_active_members` in the next lesson is materialized as a `table`, because its date-spine join is genuinely expensive to recompute on every single downstream query, and paying that cost once per `dbt run` is far cheaper than paying it on every row Power BI ever asks for.

## Step 8 — Confirm the naming convention holds before moving on

Every model in this layer starts with `stg_`, matches exactly one raw table, and lives in `models/staging/`. That consistency is what lets anyone -- including a teammate who's never opened this project before -- open the `models/` folder and immediately know which layer they're looking at and what it's allowed to do. Breaking that convention even once, by sneaking a join into a model still named `stg_something`, is exactly the kind of small inconsistency that makes a dbt project hard to trust six months later.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Staging layer is built: stg_memberships, stg_billing, stg_locations, each a thin 1:1 view over its raw Snowflake table with only renaming, type casting, and status normalization -- no business logic. All three are declared against a sources.yml block rather than hardcoded table names, and row counts reconcile exactly against the raw tables. Everything from here forward reads from staging, never from raw directly.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The first real layer of the dbt project is built on top of the raw data we landed last lesson. This is intentionally the simplest layer -- it just cleans up formatting -- so that the next lesson, where we actually define what 'active member' means, is working from clean, consistent data instead of three different teams' inconsistent raw formats.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've cleaned up the raw nightly data feed into a consistent, predictable shape inside Snowflake. Nothing about what counts as an active member has been decided yet -- that's deliberate, so the next step can define it once, correctly, instead of inheriting any hidden assumptions from this cleanup pass.

lessons.title: Building the Intermediate Model: One Definition of 'Active Member'
lessons.summary: The business-logic heart of the project -- int_active_members defines "active" once, handling paused memberships and multi-location overlap.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the single most important model in the entire Brightleaf project. `int_active_members` takes the clean `stg_memberships` data and answers, once, for every member on every day, the exact question Finance, Marketing, and Product have each been answering differently for years: is this person an active member today? We handle the two real edge cases that caused the original disagreement -- a membership paused in the middle of a month, and a member who holds overlapping memberships at two different studio locations -- so that every team downstream inherits the same answer instead of writing their own guess.

The model expands each membership's status history out across a calendar day spine, then collapses any day where a member has more than one overlapping membership row down to exactly one row per member per day. That collapsing step is what makes it safe for a mart to later `count(distinct member_id)` without silently double-counting anyone.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine three kids on a playground each keeping their own tally of "who's playing tag right now," and all three tallies disagree because one kid counts someone who went to the bathroom for five minutes as still playing, another doesn't, and a third accidentally counts a kid twice because he was standing near two different groups. The fix isn't to argue about whose tally is right -- it's to pick one kid, give them a clear rule for exactly what counts as "playing," and have everyone else just ask that one kid from now on.

`int_active_members` is that one kid with the clear rule. For every single day, for every single member, it decides -- using one agreed rule, not three different guesses -- whether that person counts as active that day, and it only ever reports each person once per day, even if they technically belong to two locations at once.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This model is built on two deliberate techniques: a date-spine join to expand status *periods* into one row per member per calendar day, and a deduplication pass using a window function to collapse overlapping membership rows down to the grain of one row per `(member_id, activity_date)`. The date-spine expansion is what makes a mid-month pause visible at all -- without it, a membership that was active for twenty days and paused for the remaining ten would either be averaged into something meaningless or, worse, judged by whatever single status happened to be current on the day someone ran the query.

The multi-location overlap case is the subtler of the two: Brightleaf members who transfer studios, or who hold a secondary membership at a second location, can have two `stg_memberships` rows both claiming the same `member_id` on the same `activity_date`. Counting both rows would inflate every headcount downstream. We resolve it with a `row_number()` window partitioned by `member_id, activity_date`, ordered so an `ACTIVE` row always wins a tie against any other status, and any remaining tie breaks on the most recent `membership_id`. That ordering choice is itself a business rule worth writing down explicitly in code, because it's exactly the kind of silent decision that used to live differently inside three separate teams' SQL.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Expand each membership status period across a day spine

`stg_memberships` holds one row per status *period* (a start date and an end date, or a null end date meaning "still open"). We need one row per member per *day* to be able to say whether someone was active on any given date, including mid-month changes.

```sql
-- models/intermediate/int_active_members.sql
{{ config(materialized='table') }}

with date_spine as (

    {{ dbt_utils.date_spine(
        datepart="day",
        start_date="cast('2023-01-01' as date)",
        end_date="dateadd(day, 1, current_date())"
    ) }}

),

membership_periods as (

    select
        member_id,
        membership_id,
        location_id,
        plan_code,
        status,
        status_start_date,
        -- an open period (still active today) gets an end date one day
        -- past "today" so it joins against every day up to and including today
        coalesce(status_end_date, dateadd(day, 1, current_date())) as status_end_date_inclusive
    from {{ ref('stg_memberships') }}

),
```

## Step 2 — Join the spine to every membership that covers each day

```sql
member_day_status as (

    select
        mp.member_id,
        mp.membership_id,
        mp.location_id,
        mp.plan_code,
        mp.status,
        ds.date_day as activity_date
    from membership_periods mp
    inner join date_spine ds
        on ds.date_day >= mp.status_start_date
       and ds.date_day <  mp.status_end_date_inclusive

),
```

This is the step that makes a membership paused on, say, the 14th of the month show up as `PAUSED` for every day from the 14th onward and `ACTIVE` for every day before it -- not one status smeared across the whole month.

## Step 3 — Collapse multi-location overlap to one row per member per day

```sql
ranked as (

    select
        member_id,
        activity_date,
        membership_id,
        location_id,
        plan_code,
        status,
        row_number() over (
            partition by member_id, activity_date
            order by
                case when status = 'ACTIVE' then 0 else 1 end,
                membership_id desc
        ) as rn
    from member_day_status

)

select
    member_id,
    activity_date,
    membership_id,
    location_id,
    plan_code,
    status,
    status = 'ACTIVE' as is_active
from ranked
where rn = 1
```

If a member has one `ACTIVE` membership at Location A and one `PAUSED` secondary membership at Location B on the same day, the `ACTIVE` row wins and the member is counted once, as active, at Location A. Document that choice in plain language right next to the code -- it's a business rule, not a technical detail.

## Step 4 — Confirm the grain holds before building anything on top

```sql
select member_id, activity_date, count(*)
from {{ ref('int_active_members') }}
group by member_id, activity_date
having count(*) > 1;
-- must return zero rows
```

## Step 5 — Spot-check the two edge cases by hand

Pick one member you know was paused mid-month and one you know transferred locations, and query `int_active_members` filtered to just that `member_id` across the relevant week. Confirm the paused member's `is_active` flips to `false` exactly on the pause date, and the transferring member appears exactly once per day throughout the overlap, never twice.

## Step 6 — Materialize it as a table, deliberately

```sql
{{ config(materialized='table') }}
```

This config line at the top of the model is not incidental. The date-spine join in Step 2 expands every membership period out across potentially hundreds of day-rows, and the window function in Step 3 then re-scans that expanded set per member -- both genuinely expensive operations. Materializing as a `table` means `dbt run` pays that cost once per run and every downstream model (the two marts in Lesson 12, and anything Power BI eventually queries) reads a small, already-computed table instead of re-triggering that expansion on every single query. A `view` here would silently push a heavy computation onto every dashboard click.

## Step 7 — Write down why this logic lives here and nowhere else

Add a comment at the top of the model file stating the rule in plain language, not just in SQL: "A member is active on a day if their highest-priority membership status that day is ACTIVE; ACTIVE always wins a same-day tie against any other status." Anyone tempted to recompute 'active' differently inside a mart, a Power BI measure, or an ad-hoc query should find this comment and `ref()` this model instead -- that's the entire mechanism that prevents the original three-teams-three-answers problem from quietly coming back.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built int_active_members -- this is the model that ends the three-teams-three-numbers problem. It expands every membership status period across a daily date spine using dbt_utils.date_spine so a mid-month pause shows up on the exact day it happened, then collapses multi-location overlaps to one row per member per day with a row_number() window that prefers an active status on ties. Grain is verified with a zero-rows check before anything else gets built on it.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: This is the model the whole project exists to build. Finance, Marketing, and Product's active-member numbers have disagreed for years because each team wrote their own definition by hand; this model writes that definition exactly once, including the two specific situations -- a mid-month pause and a member at two locations -- that were causing the worst of the disagreement.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We just built the single source of truth for what counts as an active member at Brightleaf. It's built to handle the real situations that were causing your three teams' numbers to disagree -- someone pausing mid-month, someone belonging to two locations -- so that going forward, everyone is counting the same thing, the same way.

lessons.title: Writing dbt Tests That Actually Catch Problems
lessons.summary: Generic schema tests plus a custom singular test that enforces the active-member business rule itself, not just column hygiene.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
A model that defines "active member" correctly today is only useful if it keeps being correct as Brightleaf's data changes every single night. This lesson adds the tests that make that a guarantee instead of a hope: standard dbt generic tests (`unique`, `not_null`, `accepted_values`) that catch basic data-hygiene problems, plus one custom singular test that directly checks the business rule driving this whole project -- that a single membership can never be recorded as both `ACTIVE` and `PAUSED` on the same calendar day.

The generic tests catch the kind of problem any table can have. The singular test catches the kind of problem that's specific to Brightleaf's actual business logic, and it's the test that would have caught the original three-teams-disagree bug years earlier if it had existed.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a referee at a sports game with two different jobs. One job is simple rule-checking anyone could do: is the ball actually on the field? Did the player actually cross the line? That's like checking a column for null values or checking that an ID isn't duplicated -- straightforward, same for every sport.

The other job is specific to this particular game's actual rules: in this league, can a player be on the bench and on the field at the same time? No -- that's against this league's specific rules, not a general sports rule. That's the custom test we write here: a check built specifically for Brightleaf's own rule that nobody can be both active and paused at the same moment. A referee who only checked the generic stuff would miss that completely.
lessons.explainProfessional:
dbt separates tests into two real categories, and conflating them is a common mistake. Generic tests (`unique`, `not_null`, `accepted_values`, and custom generic tests reused across many models) live in YAML and check structural properties of a column -- they answer "is this data shaped correctly," not "is this data business-logic-correct." Singular tests are hand-written SQL files in the `tests/` directory that return failing rows when a specific business assertion is violated; dbt treats any non-empty result set from a test query as a failure.

For Brightleaf, the generic tests on `stg_memberships` and `int_active_members` catch malformed or missing data -- a null `member_id`, a `status` value outside the four known codes, a duplicate key. But none of those would have caught the actual historical bug: three teams each writing their own "active" logic and quietly disagreeing. That requires a test that encodes the actual business rule as a query -- an overlap self-join that returns any membership with two different status values claiming to be true on the same day. If that query ever returns rows, it means either the source system recorded something inconsistent, or a future change to `int_active_members` broke the guarantee this whole series was built to establish. Wiring this test into CI, which happens in a later lesson, means that guarantee gets checked on every single pull request, forever, not just the day it was written.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Add generic tests to the staging and intermediate layers

Most of this was started in Lesson 9 for staging. Extend it to `int_active_members`, since the model that matters most deserves the most scrutiny:

```yaml
# models/intermediate/_int__models.yml
version: 2

models:
  - name: int_active_members
    description: >
      One row per member per calendar day. The single governed definition
      of "active member" for Brightleaf Fitness -- handles mid-month
      pauses and multi-location overlap. See writtenInstructions, Lesson 10.
    columns:
      - name: member_id
        tests: [not_null]
      - name: activity_date
        tests: [not_null]
      - name: status
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['ACTIVE', 'PAUSED', 'CANCELED', 'TRIAL']
      - name: is_active
        tests: [not_null]
    tests:
      - dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns:
          combination_of_columns:
            - member_id
            - activity_date
```

That last test is the one worth pausing on: it directly verifies the dedupe logic from Lesson 10 actually worked -- exactly one row per member per day, with no duplicates slipping through from the multi-location collapse.

## Step 2 — Write the custom singular test for the business rule itself

Generic tests check column shape. This test checks the rule the whole project exists to enforce: a single membership record can never claim two different statuses on the same day.

```sql
-- tests/assert_no_overlapping_membership_statuses.sql
--
-- Business rule: one membership can never be ACTIVE and PAUSED (or any
-- two different statuses) on the same calendar day. A non-empty result
-- here means int_active_members's active-member definition cannot be
-- trusted for the affected members until the source data is fixed.

with periods as (

    select
        member_id,
        membership_id,
        status,
        status_start_date,
        coalesce(status_end_date, dateadd(day, 1, current_date())) as status_end_date_inclusive
    from {{ ref('stg_memberships') }}

)

select
    a.member_id,
    a.membership_id,
    a.status as status_a,
    b.status as status_b,
    a.status_start_date,
    a.status_end_date_inclusive
from periods a
inner join periods b
    on a.membership_id = b.membership_id
   and a.status <> b.status
   and a.status_start_date < b.status_end_date_inclusive
   and b.status_start_date < a.status_end_date_inclusive
```

This is a self-join looking for two overlapping date ranges on the same `membership_id` with different statuses. If it ever returns a row, dbt fails the build -- which is exactly the behavior we want, since this specific inconsistency is what silently produced wrong "active member" numbers for years before this project existed.

## Step 3 — Run the full test suite and read the failures as data, not noise

```
dbt test --select staging intermediate
```

If `assert_no_overlapping_membership_statuses` fails on real data, that's not a bug in the test -- it's the test doing its job and surfacing a genuine data-quality problem in the SQL Server source that nobody caught before. Route that finding back to whoever owns the membership system, don't quietly filter it out in the model.

## Step 4 — Name tests so a failure is instantly diagnosable

Rename the generated test file if needed so `dbt test` output reads `assert_no_overlapping_membership_statuses FAIL` rather than a generic `custom_sql_test_1` -- a test name should tell whoever's on call what broke without opening the file.

## Step 5 — Treat test coverage as part of "done," not an afterthought

Every new column added to `int_active_members` or either mart from here forward gets at minimum a `not_null` test, and any new business rule gets its own singular test, following this exact pattern -- a plain-English comment stating the rule, then the SQL that would catch its violation.
