More importantly, wrote a custom singular test, assert_no_overlapping_membership_statuses.sql, that self-joins stg_memberships to catch any membership recorded as two different statuses on the same day -- the exact kind of source inconsistency that caused the original three-teams-disagree problem.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've gone beyond basic data-quality checks and written a test for Brightleaf's actual business rule -- no member can be both active and paused at once. This is what turns 'we think the data is right' into something the system checks automatically, every time, instead of something someone has to remember to verify by hand.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've built an automatic check for the exact kind of inconsistency that caused your teams' numbers to disagree in the first place. If anything in the source system ever produces that same kind of contradiction again, the system catches it immediately instead of letting it quietly produce a wrong number months later.

lessons.title: Building the Mart Models and Documentation
lessons.summary: member_activity_mart and revenue_mart -- the governed tables Power BI and every team will actually query -- plus dbt docs and description fields.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This lesson builds the layer every team actually touches: the marts. `member_activity_mart` rolls `int_active_members` up to one row per member per calendar month, giving Finance, Marketing, and Product a single governed table to answer "how many active members did we have in March" without anyone writing their own SQL again. `revenue_mart` joins billing data against that same active-member foundation to produce monthly recognized revenue by location and plan.

We also add the documentation layer here: `description` fields on every mart column, and a markdown doc block explaining the active-member definition in plain language, so anyone who opens `dbt docs generate` -- not just someone who reads the model's SQL -- can see exactly what each number means and where it comes from.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the one kid on the playground who now has the official tally of who's playing tag? A mart is like that kid's older sibling taking that daily tally and making it into a monthly report card: "in March, here's how many kids played on average, broken down by which part of the playground they played in." It's built from the same trustworthy daily counts, just organized into the shape people actually want to look at -- a month at a time, not a day at a time.

We also write a little note card explaining the rule in plain words, so a parent who's never seen the tally sheet can still understand exactly how "playing" was defined, instead of having to ask the kid directly every time.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Mart models are where governed logic meets the shape business users actually consume -- monthly grain, pre-aggregated, joined to the dimensions (location, plan) a Power BI report will slice by. `member_activity_mart` aggregates `int_active_members` from a daily grain up to one row per `member_id` per calendar month, which is both a usability decision (nobody wants to filter 365 rows per member in Power BI) and a performance one (pre-aggregating in the warehouse means the BI layer isn't re-scanning a daily-grain table on every slicer change).

`revenue_mart` is built by joining `stg_billing` against the active-member foundation to attribute revenue to a location and plan for each billing period. This is also, worth being honest about, the kind of join where a grain mismatch between two tables can silently multiply rows and inflate a sum -- joining an invoice-grain table against a day-grain table on a date range, without first collapsing one side to the matching grain, is exactly the shape of a join fanout. A careful reviewer re-checking this join against the two tables' actual grains, the same discipline from Lesson 10, is in a position to catch that kind of problem before it ships. Documentation closes the loop: a `description` on `revenue_mart.total_revenue_usd` and a `{% docs %}` block defining "active member" in one place mean the mart's meaning is discoverable in `dbt docs generate`, not locked inside whoever wrote the SQL.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Build member_activity_mart

```sql
-- models/marts/member_activity_mart.sql
{{ config(materialized='table') }}

with daily_activity as (

    select * from {{ ref('int_active_members') }}

),

monthly as (

    select
        member_id,
        date_trunc('month', activity_date)      as activity_month,
        max_by(location_id, activity_date)        as location_id,
        max_by(plan_code, activity_date)            as plan_code,
        count_if(is_active)                           as days_active,
        max(is_active::int) = 1                        as was_active_any_day
    from daily_activity
    group by member_id, date_trunc('month', activity_date)

)

select
    member_id,
    activity_month,
    location_id,
    plan_code,
    days_active,
    was_active_any_day
from monthly
```

`max_by(location_id, activity_date)` picks the member's most recent location that month -- a deliberate, documented choice for members who transferred locations mid-month.

## Step 2 — Build revenue_mart

```sql
-- models/marts/revenue_mart.sql
{{ config(materialized='table') }}

with billing as (

    select * from {{ ref('stg_billing') }}

),

active_members as (

    select * from {{ ref('int_active_members') }}

),

billing_with_location as (

    select
        b.billing_id,
        b.member_id,
        b.billing_period_start,
        b.billing_period_end,
        b.amount_paid_usd,
        a.location_id,
        a.plan_code
    from billing b
    inner join active_members a
        on a.member_id = b.member_id
       and a.activity_date between b.billing_period_start and b.billing_period_end

)

select
    location_id,
    date_trunc('month', billing_period_start) as revenue_month,
    plan_code,
    sum(amount_paid_usd) as total_revenue_usd
from billing_with_location
group by 1, 2, 3
```

## Step 3 — Write a markdown doc block for the active-member definition

```markdown
{# docs/active_member_definition.md #}
{% docs active_member_definition %}

A Brightleaf member counts as **active** on a given day if their most
recent membership status record covering that day is `ACTIVE`. A member
with overlapping memberships (for example, during a studio transfer) is
counted once, preferring an `ACTIVE` status over any other status on
that day. Defined once in `int_active_members` -- see Lesson 10.

{% enddocs %}
```

## Step 4 — Add descriptions and reference the doc block in schema.yml

```yaml
# models/marts/_marts__models.yml
version: 2

models:
  - name: member_activity_mart
    description: >
      One row per member per calendar month. The governed source for any
      "how many active members" question -- see the active_member_definition
      doc block for exactly how active is defined.
    columns:
      - name: member_id
        tests: [not_null]
      - name: was_active_any_day
        description: '{{ doc("active_member_definition") }}'

  - name: revenue_mart
    description: >
      One row per location, per month, per plan. Recognized revenue
      attributed using the same active-member foundation as
      member_activity_mart, so revenue and headcount numbers are always
      traceable to the same underlying definition.
    columns:
      - name: total_revenue_usd
        description: Sum of amount_paid_usd for invoices whose billing period overlaps an active-member day at that location.
```

## Step 5 — Generate and review the docs site

```
dbt docs generate
dbt docs serve
```

Open the lineage graph and confirm it traces cleanly: `raw.sql_server_memberships` -> `stg_memberships` -> `int_active_members` -> `member_activity_mart` and `revenue_mart`. Click into `revenue_mart` and re-read its join against `int_active_members` one more time, checking each table's actual grain against the other -- a day-grain table joined to an invoice-grain table on a date range is exactly the shape worth double-checking before this ships to Power BI.

## Step 6 — Add basic schema tests to both marts before calling them done

Marts inherit correctness from the layers underneath them, but they still need their own guardrails:

```yaml
  - name: member_activity_mart
    tests:
      - dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns:
          combination_of_columns:
            - member_id
            - activity_month
  - name: revenue_mart
    columns:
      - name: total_revenue_usd
        tests:
          - dbt_utils.accepted_range:
              min_value: 0
```

The uniqueness test on `member_activity_mart` confirms the monthly aggregation in Step 1 didn't accidentally produce duplicate member-month rows, and the non-negative check on `total_revenue_usd` is a cheap sanity floor -- revenue should never come back negative from a straightforward sum of paid amounts.

## Step 7 — Decide materialization for both marts

Both marts are configured `materialized='table'`, matching `int_active_members`. These are the tables Power BI connects to directly, refreshed once per `dbt run` rather than recomputed on every report open -- the same reasoning from Lesson 10, now one layer further downstream, where the audience querying them has grown from one pipeline to three entire business teams.

Added descriptions on every mart column and a {% docs %} block defining 'active member' in plain language, so dbt docs generate gives a non-technical reader the real definition, not just a column list.

lessons.title: Setting Up CI: dbt Build on Every Pull Request
lessons.summary: Wiring GitHub Actions to run dbt build and dbt test against a Snowflake CI schema on every pull request, so a broken model can't merge.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Every model and test built over the last five lessons — staging, `int_active_members`, `member_activity_mart`, `revenue_mart` — only gets checked when someone remembers to run `dbt build` by hand before merging. This lesson wires that check into GitHub itself: a GitHub Actions workflow that automatically runs `dbt deps`, `dbt build`, and `dbt test` against a dedicated Snowflake CI schema on every pull request that touches a model, test, or macro. If anything fails, the pull request shows a red X and cannot be merged — nobody has to remember to run the tests, because the robot already ran them and already said no.

This also puts a second, mechanical guarantee behind the human one from Lessons 9 through 12. Finance, Marketing, and Product all query the same governed marts now; this workflow is what keeps a future pull request from quietly weakening the active-member business rule and three teams' numbers going wrong a week later, instead of the problem showing up on the pull request itself, before it ever reaches a shared schema.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a strict hall monitor who checks every single homework assignment before it's allowed into the class turn-in bin — not after. If problem 3 has the wrong answer, the monitor hands it straight back to you instead of letting it sit in the bin with everyone else's finished work. That is what we are building: a robot monitor that checks every proposed change to our data models before it is allowed anywhere near the real data everyone at the company relies on.

The robot does its checking by actually building a small practice copy of the whole data model and running every test against that practice copy, every single time someone proposes a change — not once a week, not when someone remembers, every time, automatically.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is continuous integration applied to an analytics-engineering codebase, and the mechanism that matters is isolation: every pull request triggers a dbt build against its own disposable Snowflake schema, never against the shared `dev` or `prod` schemas. GitHub Actions checks out the PR branch, installs the `dbt-snowflake` adapter, runs `dbt deps` to pull `dbt_utils` (needed for several of the generic tests from Lesson 10), then `dbt build --target ci`, which compiles and materializes every model from staging through the marts fresh, inside a schema named for the PR number so concurrent pull requests can never collide or clobber each other's runs.

`dbt test` then runs as its own explicit step, separate from `dbt build`, so the PR's status checks show "did it compile" and "did the data pass the rules" as two distinguishable signals rather than one combined log a reviewer has to dig through. The CI service account is scoped to read/write only the `PR_*` schema pattern on a small CI-sized warehouse — it has no access to the schemas `int_active_members` and the marts actually live in, so even a badly broken pull request can only ever damage its own disposable sandbox.

Branch protection on `main` is what makes this binding rather than advisory: the `dbt-build-and-test` check is marked as a required status check, so GitHub itself disables the merge button until it passes. That one setting is what actually closes the loop between "we wrote tests in Lessons 9 through 12" and "a broken model literally cannot reach the schemas Finance, Marketing, and Product query."
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Decide exactly what the CI run has to isolate

Before writing any YAML, settle three things: CI builds into a schema named after the pull request (`PR_482`), under a dedicated warehouse (`BRIGHTLEAF_CI_WH`) sized small since it only ever processes a few days of sample-sized seed data, using a role (`TRANSFORMER_CI`) that can create and drop schemas matching `PR_*` and nothing else. None of this role's grants touch the schemas the marts live in.

## Step 2 — Add a CI target to the dbt profile

```
# ci/profiles.yml
brightleaf_analytics:
  target: ci
  outputs:
    ci:
      type: snowflake
      account: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT') }}"
      user: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_USER') }}"
      password: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD') }}"
      role: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_ROLE') }}"
      warehouse: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_WAREHOUSE') }}"
      database: "{{ env_var('SNOWFLAKE_DATABASE') }}"
      schema: "{{ env_var('DBT_CI_SCHEMA') }}"
      threads: 4
```

Every value comes from an environment variable — nothing in this file is a real credential, so it is safe to commit.

## Step 3 — Write the GitHub Actions workflow

```
# .github/workflows/dbt_ci.yml
name: dbt CI

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - "models/**"
      - "tests/**"
      - "macros/**"
      - "dbt_project.yml"
      - "packages.yml"

concurrency:
  group: dbt-ci-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  dbt-build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: ci
    env:
      DBT_PROFILES_DIR: ./ci
      SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT }}
      SNOWFLAKE_USER: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_CI_USER }}
      SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_CI_PASSWORD }}
      SNOWFLAKE_ROLE: TRANSFORMER_CI
      SNOWFLAKE_WAREHOUSE: BRIGHTLEAF_CI_WH
      SNOWFLAKE_DATABASE: BRIGHTLEAF_ANALYTICS
      DBT_CI_SCHEMA: PR_${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
    steps:
      - name: Check out PR branch
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"

      - name: Install dbt
        run: pip install dbt-snowflake==1.8.0

      - name: dbt deps
        run: dbt deps

      - name: dbt build (CI schema)
        run: dbt build --target ci --fail-fast

      - name: dbt test (explicit status check)
        if: always()
        run: dbt test --target ci

      - name: Drop the CI schema
        if: always()
        run: python scripts/drop_ci_schema.py "$DBT_CI_SCHEMA"
```

`--fail-fast` stops the build at the first failing model instead of grinding through the whole DAG, which keeps a broken PR's feedback fast. The final cleanup step runs `if: always()` specifically so a failed build still drops its scratch schema instead of leaving `PR_482` sitting in Snowflake forever.

## Step 4 — Store the Snowflake credentials as repository secrets

In GitHub, under Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions, add `SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT`, `SNOWFLAKE_CI_USER`, and `SNOWFLAKE_CI_PASSWORD` — scoped to the `TRANSFORMER_CI` role created in Step 1, never a personal or admin login.

## Step 5 — Make the check a merge gate, not just a nice-to-have

In Settings > Branches, add a protection rule on `main` requiring the `dbt-build-and-test` status check to pass before merging, and requiring branches to be up to date before merge. This is the setting that turns "we have CI" into "a broken model cannot reach `main`" — without it, a red X is just a comment someone can ignore.

## Step 6 — Prove it actually blocks something

Open a throwaway pull request that changes `int_active_members` to intentionally violate one of the generic tests from Lesson 10 — for example, drop the `not_null` test on `member_id`. Push it, watch the Action run, and confirm the PR page shows the check failed and the merge button is disabled. Then revert the change and confirm the same PR goes green. Seeing it actually block a real failure, once, is worth more than reading the YAML twice.

## Step 7 — Watch the next few real pull requests, not just the test one

A deliberately broken test PR proves the mechanism works; it doesn't prove the workflow is actually fast and reliable enough for people to trust day to day. Keep an eye on the Actions tab for the first handful of real pull requests that follow — confirm the CI schema actually drops every time (check Snowflake for orphaned `PR_*` schemas after a few days), and confirm the full run finishes in a time nobody's tempted to skip by merging without waiting. A CI check that takes fifteen minutes on a project this size, or leaves scratch schemas behind, invites exactly the workaround — "just merge it, CI's slow today" — that this whole lesson exists to make unnecessary.
