Made the dbt-build-and-test check a required status on main, and proved it actually blocks a merge by pushing a deliberately broken PR before merging this.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Every change to the data models now gets automatically tested before it can be merged, not whenever someone remembers to run it by hand. That protects the three teams already relying on these models from a future change quietly breaking the active-member logic without anyone noticing until it's live.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've added an automatic safety check that tests every proposed change to the reporting logic before it's allowed to go live, the same way code gets reviewed before shipping at a mature software company. A mistake now gets caught in minutes, on the proposed change itself, instead of surfacing later as a wrong number in someone's report.

lessons.title: Orchestrating the Pipeline With Airflow
lessons.summary: Building the Airflow DAG that extracts from SQL Server, then runs dbt build and test, every night on a schedule with failure alerting.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
CI now protects every change to the dbt project, but something still has to actually run the pipeline every night — pulling fresh rows out of the legacy SQL Server database and then building the warehouse on top of them. This lesson builds that something: an Airflow DAG, `brightleaf_nightly_pipeline`, that runs the Python extraction script against SQL Server, lands the results in Snowflake's `raw` schema, then triggers `dbt run` and `dbt test` in that order — with an alert that fires the moment any one of those three steps fails.

This is the piece that makes everything built in Lessons 8 through 12 actually happen on its own, every night, without anyone opening a terminal. Finance, Marketing, and Product only trust one governed number if that number is reliably fresh every morning — orchestration is what turns a correct pipeline into an operational one.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a relay race with three runners: the first one runs to get the baton (extract the data), the second one runs it most of the way (build the models), and the third one checks it crossed the finish line correctly (test the results). Airflow is the race official standing at the side with a clipboard, making sure each runner starts only after the one before them has actually finished — and blowing a whistle loudly if any one of them trips, instead of just quietly noticing and saying nothing.

Every single night, without anyone waking up to press "go," this relay runs on its own, in the same order, at the same time, so the data is always ready before anyone needs to look at it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is pipeline orchestration, and the design choice that matters most is making the dependency chain explicit rather than implicit. The DAG has three tasks wired with `>>`: `extract_sql_server_to_snowflake` (a `PythonOperator` calling the extraction script against SQL Server for `memberships`, `billing`, and `locations`), then `dbt_run` (a `BashOperator` invoking `dbt run --target prod --select tag:nightly`), then `dbt_test` (`dbt test` against the same selection). Airflow guarantees `dbt_run` cannot start until extraction reports success, and `dbt_test` cannot start until the models actually built — which matters because testing stale or half-loaded data would produce a false pass that looks exactly like a real one.

The schedule, `0 2 * * *`, runs after Brightleaf's own SQL Server nightly batch jobs close out but comfortably ahead of the morning hours Finance, Marketing, and Product start pulling from the marts. `max_active_runs=1` and `catchup=False` prevent two nights' runs from ever overlapping or Airflow trying to silently backfill every missed day if the scheduler was down — both failure modes that look fine in a demo and cause real damage the first time a server reboots at the wrong moment.

Failure alerting is wired as its own task, `alert_pipeline_failure`, downstream of all three pipeline tasks with `trigger_rule="one_failed"` — it only fires if at least one upstream task actually failed, and it fires regardless of which one, so a failure anywhere in the chain reaches a human rather than failing silently into a log nobody reads until Finance asks why yesterday's numbers look wrong.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Decide the task boundaries before writing the DAG

Three tasks, one clear dependency chain: extract SQL Server into Snowflake's `raw` schema, run the dbt models tagged `nightly`, then test them. Each task should fail loudly and stop the chain rather than let a downstream task start against incomplete data.

## Step 2 — Write the extraction callable

The extraction script already exists from earlier in this series — it connects to the on-premises SQL Server instance, pulls `memberships`, `billing`, and `locations`, and writes them into `raw.sql_server_memberships`, `raw.sql_server_billing`, and `raw.sql_server_locations` in Snowflake. Wrap it in a function Airflow can call directly:

```
# dags/scripts/extract_sql_server.py
def run_extraction(tables, target_schema):
    for table in tables:
        rows = pull_from_sql_server(table)
        load_to_snowflake(rows, schema=target_schema, table=f"sql_server_{table}")
        if rows_loaded_count(table) == 0:
            raise ValueError(f"Extraction for {table} returned zero rows — refusing to continue.")
```

Raising on a zero-row extraction matters: a connection that silently returns nothing should stop the DAG, not quietly hand `dbt_run` an empty `raw` table and let it build on top of yesterday's stale data without anyone noticing.

## Step 3 — Build the DAG

```
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator
from airflow.operators.email import EmailOperator
from airflow.utils.trigger_rule import TriggerRule
from scripts.extract_sql_server import run_extraction

default_args = {
    "owner": "analytics-engineering",
    "retries": 2,
    "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5),
}

with DAG(
    dag_id="brightleaf_nightly_pipeline",
    default_args=default_args,
    schedule_interval="0 2 * * *",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 9, 1),
    catchup=False,
    max_active_runs=1,
    tags=["brightleaf", "dbt", "snowflake"],
) as dag:

    extract_sql_server = PythonOperator(
        task_id="extract_sql_server_to_snowflake",
        python_callable=run_extraction,
        op_kwargs={"tables": ["memberships", "billing", "locations"], "target_schema": "raw"},
    )

    dbt_run = BashOperator(
        task_id="dbt_run",
        bash_command="cd /opt/dbt/brightleaf_analytics && dbt run --target prod --select tag:nightly",
    )

    dbt_test = BashOperator(
        task_id="dbt_test",
        bash_command="cd /opt/dbt/brightleaf_analytics && dbt test --target prod --select tag:nightly",
    )

    alert_pipeline_failure = EmailOperator(
        task_id="alert_pipeline_failure",
        to="data-platform-alerts@brightleaffitness.com",
        subject="Brightleaf nightly pipeline FAILED — {{ ds }}",
        html_content="Run {{ dag_run.run_id }} failed. Check extract_sql_server_to_snowflake, dbt_run, and dbt_test in Airflow.",
        trigger_rule=TriggerRule.ONE_FAILED,
    )

    extract_sql_server >> dbt_run >> dbt_test
    [extract_sql_server, dbt_run, dbt_test] >> alert_pipeline_failure
```

## Step 4 — Tag the nightly models in dbt

```
# models/marts/revenue_mart.yml
models:
  - name: revenue_mart
    config:
      tags: ["nightly"]
```

Tagging lets `--select tag:nightly` run exactly the models this pipeline owns, without accidentally pulling in one-off or analyst-authored models that shouldn't run unattended at 2am.

## Step 5 — Set retries for the transient failure, not the real one

The `retries: 2` default on the extraction task covers a SQL Server connection blip — a brief network hiccup, not a genuine schema problem. `dbt_run` and `dbt_test` intentionally do not get the same generous retry count, because a model that fails to build or a test that fails almost never fixes itself on a second try; retrying it just delays the alert.

## Step 6 — Test the whole chain with a deliberate failure

Trigger the DAG manually from the Airflow UI, then rename a column the extraction script expects, mid-run, to force `extract_sql_server_to_snowflake` to fail. Confirm `dbt_run` and `dbt_test` both show as skipped — not run against stale data — and that `alert_pipeline_failure` fires. Revert the column and re-run to confirm a clean pass end to end.

## Step 7 — Confirm Finance, Marketing, and Product never see a half-finished night

The failure test in Step 6 matters beyond proving the alert works: it proves that a bad night never leaves the marts in a half-updated state that looks fresher than it is. Because `dbt_run` only runs after extraction succeeds, and `dbt_test` only runs after `dbt_run` succeeds, a failure anywhere in the chain means the marts simply keep yesterday's last-known-good data — stale, but not silently wrong — until someone responds to the alert and the DAG is cleared to run again. That's the same fail-loud, never-silently-wrong principle the active-member business rule itself was built on back in Lessons 9 through 11, now extended to the schedule that runs it.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built the Airflow DAG orchestrating the nightly pipeline end to end: extract SQL Server into raw, then dbt run, then dbt test, each one gated on the previous task's success so dbt never tests against a half-loaded or stale raw layer. Scheduled for 2am with max_active_runs=1 and catchup=False to avoid overlapping or silently backfilling runs, and wired a failure alert that fires off any of the three tasks, not just the last one.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The pipeline now runs itself every night, in the right order, with nobody needing to kick it off by hand. If any step fails — pulling from SQL Server, building the models, or testing them — the team gets alerted immediately instead of finding out because a report looks wrong the next morning.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The whole reporting pipeline now runs automatically every night on a schedule, and if anything goes wrong at any step, the team is alerted right away rather than finding out when someone notices a number looks off. This is what makes 'one governed number' something you can actually count on seeing fresh every morning, not just something that was true the day we built it.

lessons.title: The Active-Member Count Still Didn't Match Finance
lessons.summary: Finance says the number still doesn't match — tracing it layer by layer finds the headcount is actually fine, and a far bigger problem hiding in the revenue figure right next to it.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Twelve lessons of staging models, one governed `int_active_members` definition, generic and singular tests, CI, and nightly Airflow orchestration later, Finance comes back with the same complaint they opened the project with: "the new number still doesn't match ours." The easy, wrong move is to assume Finance's old SQL Server query is the one that's out of date — it's the ad hoc logic this whole project exists to replace, after all. This lesson resists that instinct and verifies the new number the same way you'd verify anyone else's: get both exact numbers for the exact same point in time, and trace the pipeline layer by layer until you can say precisely where — if anywhere — they actually disagree.

What the investigation finds isn't quite what it looks like at first. The member-count comparison turns out to be comparing two genuinely different questions, not two different answers to the same question — and once that's untangled, the real, serious discrepancy turns up somewhere nobody was looking: the dollar figure sitting right next to that member count, in the same report.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you ask two friends how many kids are at the park "right now," and one says 20 and the other says 35. Before deciding either friend miscounted, you'd want to ask exactly what each of them meant — did one of them count every kid who showed up for even five minutes all afternoon, while the other only counted the ones standing there at the exact moment you asked? Those are two different questions with two different honest answers, not one right count and one wrong one.

That's exactly what happens here with the member count — and once that mix-up gets sorted out, a much bigger problem turns up hiding right next to it: the money total for the same report, which is nowhere close to being right.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is data-validation discipline applied to your own pipeline, and the rule is: never assume the newer, more rigorous system is right without independently checking it against the exact same question the older system answered. Finance's legacy SQL Server query is a point-in-time count — active members as of a specific date, September 30th — and it returns 41,920. The figure Finance was actually comparing it against came from `member_activity_mart`'s `was_active_any_day` flag for September, which answers a meaningfully different question: anyone active on *any* day that month, including a member who joined on the 3rd and canceled on the 22nd. That number is 43,588, and the gap between the two is not a bug — it's two correct answers to two different questions, confirmed by re-running the comparison against `int_active_members` filtered to the single date Finance actually used (`activity_date = '2026-09-30' and is_active`), which returns 41,920 — an exact match.

That result matters for a reason beyond closing out this one complaint: it confirms the governed active-member logic, tested back in Lessons 10 and 11, is correct at its actual grain. It also means the investigation isn't over — Finance's original complaint was about the full monthly report, not just the headcount line, and the same report has a revenue figure sitting right next to it. Summing `stg_billing` directly for September and comparing it to `revenue_mart`'s total for the same month surfaces something far more serious than a definitional mismatch: the mart's number is roughly thirty times higher than the raw billing records actually support, which is not explainable by any difference in what question is being asked.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Get Finance's exact number, exact query, and exact date — don't paraphrase it

```sql
-- Finance's own legacy query, run directly against SQL Server, for 2026-09-30
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT member_id) FROM memberships
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
  AND status_start_date <= '2026-09-30'
  AND (status_end_date IS NULL OR status_end_date > '2026-09-30');
-- 41,920
```

Then get the exact number they were comparing it to on the new dashboard:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM member_activity_mart
WHERE activity_month = '2026-09-01' AND was_active_any_day;
-- 43,588
```

## Step 2 — Before chasing a bug, check whether these are even the same question

Finance's query is a point-in-time snapshot: active as of one specific date. `was_active_any_day` is a monthly flag: active on *any* day that month, which will always be greater than or equal to a single-day snapshot, since it also counts members who joined mid-month and later canceled. That difference alone could fully explain a gap this size — so test it directly instead of guessing.

## Step 3 — Re-run the comparison at the same grain Finance actually used

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM int_active_members
WHERE activity_date = '2026-09-30' AND is_active;
-- 41,920
```

An exact match. `int_active_members` is the governed, tested, per-day source of truth from Lesson 10 — queried at the same single date Finance used, it agrees with Finance's number down to the member. The headcount mismatch is closed: it was a comparison between two different definitions, not a pipeline bug, and the underlying business logic is confirmed correct.

## Step 4 — Don't stop at "the headcount is fine" — Finance's complaint was about the whole report

Finance's monthly report shows active members *and* total revenue side by side. Headcount just cleared; sanity-check revenue with the same rigor before calling this closed:

```sql
-- Hand-summed from the raw billing records, for September 2026
SELECT SUM(amount_paid_usd) FROM stg_billing
WHERE date_trunc('month', billing_period_start) = '2026-09-01';
-- $1,285,340

-- What revenue_mart actually reports for the same month
SELECT SUM(total_revenue_usd) FROM revenue_mart
WHERE revenue_month = '2026-09-01';
-- $37,966,830
```

Roughly 29.5 times higher. This is not a rounding difference or a definition mismatch like Step 2 — it's a real, serious discrepancy, and it's in the dollar figure, not the member count anyone was originally worried about.

## Step 5 — Spot-check one real invoice by hand to see the mechanism start to show

```sql
SELECT * FROM stg_billing WHERE billing_id = 'B-55210';
-- 1 row: member_id = 'M-10482', billing_period_start = '2026-09-01',
--        billing_period_end = '2026-09-30', amount_paid_usd = 49.00
```

One invoice, one member, forty-nine dollars. Now check how many rows that same invoice turns into inside `revenue_mart`'s own join logic, by running the mart's join directly as a standalone query filtered to this one invoice:

```sql
SELECT b.billing_id, count(*) AS matched_rows
FROM {{ ref('stg_billing') }} b
INNER JOIN {{ ref('int_active_members') }} a
    ON a.member_id = b.member_id
   AND a.activity_date BETWEEN b.billing_period_start AND b.billing_period_end
WHERE b.billing_id = 'B-55210'
GROUP BY b.billing_id;
-- billing_id   matched_rows
-- B-55210       30
```

One $49.00 invoice is matching thirty rows before it ever reaches the `SUM()`. That number — thirty — is not a coincidence, and it's exactly where Lesson 16 picks up.

## Step 6 — Name exactly what's proven before moving on

```
PROVEN: the active-member headcount mismatch was a comparison artifact --
        two different questions, not a bug. int_active_members and Finance
        agree exactly at the same grain.
PROVEN: revenue_mart's September total is ~29.5x the hand-summed billing
        total -- a real, serious discrepancy.
PROVEN: a single invoice is matching roughly 30 rows somewhere in
        revenue_mart's own join, before the final SUM.
NOT YET PROVEN: the exact line of SQL responsible, and why it's 30 rows
        specifically, not some other number.
```

Lesson 16 reads `revenue_mart`'s actual SQL next, and that "30" turns out to be the most important clue in the whole investigation.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Chased down Finance's 'still doesn't match' complaint and found two separate things. The headcount gap was a comparison artifact — Finance's point-in-time snapshot versus the mart's any-day-in-month flag — and resolves to an exact match once compared at the same grain, which also confirms int_active_members's logic is correct. The real problem is revenue: revenue_mart's September total is about 29.5x the hand-summed billing total, and a single spot-checked invoice is matching roughly 30 rows somewhere in the mart's join logic before the SUM runs. Haven't read the exact SQL yet, but I know the number to look for.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Finance's complaint turned out to be two different issues bundled together. The member count was never actually wrong — it was two different questions being compared — and that's now confirmed and documented. The real issue is the revenue figure, which is significantly overstated. We've isolated it to a specific calculation and know what to fix next.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We dug into Finance's concern and found good news and a real issue. The active-member count was never actually incorrect — it turned out to be two different measurements being compared, and that's now cleared up. We did find a genuine problem with the revenue number, which has been running far too high, and we know exactly where it's coming from. It will be corrected before this report goes to anyone else.

lessons.title: Finding and Fixing a Join Fanout That Inflated Revenue
lessons.summary: Reading revenue_mart's real SQL to find why one invoice was matching thirty rows before the SUM ran, fixing the grain mismatch, and adding a test to catch it if it ever comes back.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 15 proved the active-member headcount was fine and narrowed the real problem down to one exact, measurable clue: a single $49.00 invoice was matching roughly thirty rows somewhere inside `revenue_mart`'s own join logic, before any dollar figure got added up. This lesson reads that model's real SQL, finds the exact line responsible — a join matching one billing record against every calendar day in `int_active_members` instead of once — and fixes it by joining against a mart that's already at the right grain.

By the end of this lesson, `revenue_mart`'s September total drops from a number that was off by a factor of nearly thirty to one that matches a hand-summed total of the raw billing records exactly, and there's a new dbt test in place whose entire job is making sure this specific mistake can never silently reappear.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine ringing up one $49 gym membership payment on a cash register, but the register is wired to a calendar instead of a receipt printer — so it prints out one receipt for every single day of the month that payment covers, thirty receipts instead of one, all for the same forty-nine dollars. Add up all those receipts at the end of the month and it looks like that one customer paid thirty times what they actually did.

That's almost exactly what was happening. A step in the pipeline was matching one real payment against a whole month's worth of daily membership records instead of matching it just once, so every dollar got counted around thirty times before anyone added anything up. The fix is making sure each payment only ever gets matched to one record — not thirty — before the total gets calculated.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The root cause is a fan-out join, but not the usual "member has two rows" shape — it's a grain mismatch. `revenue_mart`'s `billing_with_location` CTE (built in Lesson 12) joins `stg_billing`, which has one row per invoice per billing period — roughly one row per member per month — directly against `int_active_members`, which has one row per member per *calendar day* by design, using a range condition: `a.activity_date between b.billing_period_start and b.billing_period_end`. Every invoice therefore matches one row for every day it overlaps — typically 28 to 31 rows for a standard monthly billing period — before the final `group by` and `sum(amount_paid_usd)` ever run. The `SUM()` isn't wrong about what it's adding; it's being handed the same $49.00 roughly thirty times because the row carrying that amount got duplicated thirty times by the join above it.

The diagnostic move from Lesson 15 — counting matched rows per `billing_id` before aggregation — turns what felt like "the number feels off" into an exact, provable multiplier: thirty rows for a thirty-day September billing period, twenty-eight for February, consistent with the join matching one row per calendar day in the period rather than one row per invoice. That consistency is itself the proof: a real data-quality problem, like duplicate billing records, would produce an inconsistent multiplier from member to member; a join against the wrong grain produces a multiplier that tracks the calendar almost exactly, which is the signature of a grain mismatch, not dirty data.

The fix doesn't require touching `int_active_members` or `stg_billing` at all — it requires joining billing against something that's actually at the member-per-month grain, which `member_activity_mart`, built one lesson earlier for an unrelated reason, already is. Swapping the join target from the day-grain `int_active_members` to the month-grain `member_activity_mart`, and matching on `member_id` plus the billing period's month rather than a day-range `BETWEEN`, makes the join one-to-one by construction — there is no fanout left for a `SUM()` to be fooled by, because there's nothing left to multiply against.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Read revenue_mart's actual join, with the "30" from Lesson 15 in mind

```sql
-- models/marts/revenue_mart.sql (BEFORE -- the bug, as built in Lesson 12)
with billing as (
    select * from {{ ref('stg_billing') }}
),
active_members as (
    select * from {{ ref('int_active_members') }}
),
billing_with_location as (
    select
        b.billing_id, b.member_id, b.billing_period_start, b.billing_period_end,
        b.amount_paid_usd, a.location_id, a.plan_code
    from billing b
    inner join active_members a
        on a.member_id = b.member_id
       and a.activity_date between b.billing_period_start and b.billing_period_end
)
select
    location_id,
    date_trunc('month', billing_period_start) as revenue_month,
    plan_code,
    sum(amount_paid_usd) as total_revenue_usd
from billing_with_location
group by 1, 2, 3
```

`billing` has one row per invoice, roughly one per member per month. `active_members` (`int_active_members`) has one row per member per *calendar day*, by design, from Lesson 10. The join condition matches every day the billing period overlaps — not one row, a whole month of them — which is exactly the grain mismatch Lesson 15's spot-check caught in the act.

## Step 2 — Confirm the multiplier tracks the calendar, which rules out dirty data

```sql
select
    b.billing_id,
    datediff(day, b.billing_period_start, b.billing_period_end) + 1 as period_length_days,
    count(*) as matched_rows
from {{ ref('stg_billing') }} b
inner join {{ ref('int_active_members') }} a
    on a.member_id = b.member_id
   and a.activity_date between b.billing_period_start and b.billing_period_end
group by 1, 2
order by matched_rows desc
limit 10;
```

```
billing_id   period_length_days   matched_rows
B-55210       30                    30
B-61094        31                    31
B-50218         28                    28
```

`matched_rows` equals `period_length_days` for every invoice checked, not a random or inconsistent number. A real duplicate-record problem wouldn't line up with the calendar this cleanly — this is a join matching one row per day, structurally, not a data-quality defect.

## Step 3 — Fix it: join against a mart that's already at the right grain

`member_activity_mart`, built in Lesson 12 for an unrelated reason, is already one row per member per calendar month with `location_id` and `plan_code` resolved. Join billing against that instead of against the day-grain `int_active_members`, matching on the month rather than a day-range:

```sql
-- models/marts/revenue_mart.sql (AFTER -- the fix)
with billing as (
    select * from {{ ref('stg_billing') }}
),
member_month as (
    select member_id, activity_month, location_id, plan_code
    from {{ ref('member_activity_mart') }}
),
billing_with_location as (
    select
        b.billing_id,
        b.member_id,
        b.billing_period_start,
        b.amount_paid_usd,
        mm.location_id,
        mm.plan_code
    from billing b
    inner join member_month mm
        on mm.member_id = b.member_id
       and mm.activity_month = date_trunc('month', b.billing_period_start)
)
select
    location_id,
    date_trunc('month', billing_period_start) as revenue_month,
    plan_code,
    sum(amount_paid_usd) as total_revenue_usd
from billing_with_location
group by 1, 2, 3
```

`member_month` is one row per member per month by construction, so one invoice now matches exactly one row, every time — there's no day-grain table left on the other side of the join for a billing record to fan out against.

## Step 4 — Rebuild and reconcile against the hand-summed total from Lesson 15

```
dbt run --select revenue_mart
dbt test --select revenue_mart
```

```sql
SELECT SUM(total_revenue_usd) FROM revenue_mart
WHERE revenue_month = '2026-09-01';
-- $1,285,340
```

Matches the hand-summed `stg_billing` total from Lesson 15, Step 4, exactly — down from $37,966,830 to $1,285,340.

## Step 5 — Add a regression test that encodes the actual invariant that broke

The real rule this bug violated is "one invoice contributes exactly one matched row," which a count-based test can check directly against the join grain, not just the mart's final shape:

```sql
-- tests/assert_revenue_mart_billing_join_has_no_fanout.sql
--
-- Each billing_id must match exactly one row in revenue_mart's join to
-- member-month data. A non-empty result means the join is multiplying
-- an invoice across more than one row again -- exactly the Lesson 16 bug.

select
    b.billing_id,
    count(*) as matched_rows
from {{ ref('stg_billing') }} b
inner join {{ ref('member_activity_mart') }} mm
    on mm.member_id = b.member_id
   and mm.activity_month = date_trunc('month', b.billing_period_start)
group by b.billing_id
having count(*) > 1
```

A singular test that must return zero rows — add it to the project and confirm `dbt test --select revenue_mart` now passes clean. This test, not just the fixed SQL, is what makes sure a future refactor of `revenue_mart` can't quietly reintroduce the same grain mismatch without the build failing.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Root cause: revenue_mart's billing join matched int_active_members on a day-range BETWEEN, but int_active_members is one row per member per calendar day by design -- so every invoice matched roughly 30 rows (one per day of the billing period) before the SUM ran, inflating September's revenue by about 29.5x. Confirmed it wasn't dirty data by showing the matched-row count tracked the billing period's exact day count for every invoice checked. Fixed it by joining against member_activity_mart instead, which is already one row per member per month, matching on month rather than a day range. Added a singular test asserting each invoice matches exactly one row in that join, so this exact grain mismatch can't silently come back.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Found and fixed the real cause of the revenue discrepancy: a join was unintentionally matching each invoice against a whole month of daily records instead of once, inflating revenue by close to 30 times. It's corrected, the number now matches a hand-check of the raw billing records exactly, and we've added an automatic test specifically designed to catch this exact mistake if it's ever reintroduced.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We found the real cause of the revenue number being too high: a technical join was accidentally counting each payment about thirty times over. It's fixed, the number now matches your own billing records exactly, and we've put a permanent safeguard in place so this specific mistake can't happen again without us catching it immediately.

lessons.title: Connecting Power BI to the Governed Marts
lessons.summary: Rebuilding Power BI on top of member_activity_mart and revenue_mart instead of three teams' ad-hoc queries, and setting a retirement date for the reports that started the whole problem.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Finance, Marketing, and Product never shared a dashboard — they each had their own Power BI file pointed at their own hand-written SQL Server query, which is exactly how this project started: three different "active member" counts feeding three different reports nobody trusted. This video replaces all three with one Power BI semantic model built directly on `member_activity_mart` and `revenue_mart` in Snowflake — the governed, tested, documented marts from the earlier lessons — so every visual anyone builds from here forward inherits the same validated business logic instead of re-deriving it.

This isn't a cosmetic swap of one data source for another. It's the moment the semantic layer actually becomes the thing people look at every day, which means getting a handful of modeling decisions right: how Power BI connects to Snowflake, which relationships it's allowed to draw, and — most importantly — refusing to let a DAX measure quietly redefine "active member" a fourth time.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine three friends who each kept score for the same basketball game on their own notepad, and at the end of the game they all had different final scores. The fix isn't to argue about whose notepad is right — it's to agree on one official scoreboard that everyone looks at, one that was already checked carefully to make sure it's counting the game correctly.

That's what we're building here. Power BI is the scoreboard everyone looks at, but instead of connecting it to three different homemade notepads, we're wiring it straight into the one scorebook — `member_activity_mart` and `revenue_mart` — that was already checked, tested, and fixed to count things the right way.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The modeling decisions here matter because Power BI is exactly where governance quietly dies on most analytics teams — a developer drags in a fact table, writes a measure with their own filter logic, and a fourth definition of "active member" is born, undoing everything the dbt layer enforced. The discipline is to make every measure a thin, literal pass-through of what the mart already computed, so the semantic layer has exactly one place where "active" is decided, and Power BI is not it.

We connect in Import mode rather than DirectQuery: the marts refresh nightly from the dbt job, not continuously, so there's no latency benefit to querying Snowflake live, and Import mode gives faster visuals and lets the model's relationships — `revenue_mart` and `member_activity_mart` both relating many-to-one to a slim `dim_locations` table — do the filtering instead of a query being re-issued per click. The last piece is organizational, not technical: Finance's, Marketing's, and Product's three legacy PBIX files get a formal retirement date, not a quiet deprecation, because a stale report left running next to the new one is how a fourth number quietly reappears six months from now.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Inventory what the three old reports actually computed

Before building anything new, pull up Finance's, Marketing's, and Product's existing Power BI files and write down the actual logic behind each one's "active member" number, in plain terms:

```
Finance's old report:   active = has a successful billing charge in the last 30 days
Marketing's old report: active = account status = 'active' in the membership table
                         (ignores billing entirely)
Product's old report:   active = logged a check-in via the app in the last 14 days
```

All three are reasonable-sounding and all three disagree, which is the entire reason this project exists. Keep this list — it's the exhibit you'll use in the next lesson's meeting to explain why the new number differs from each team's old one.

## Step 2 — Connect Power BI to Snowflake in Import mode

In Power BI Desktop, Get Data > Snowflake, point it at the role and database that exposes the `marts` schema, and select only three objects: `member_activity_mart`, `revenue_mart`, and a slim `dim_locations` table (location_id, location_name, region, open_date). Leave the connectivity mode on **Import**, not DirectQuery — these marts refresh once a night from the dbt job, so there is no freshness benefit to querying Snowflake live, only extra query cost and slower visuals.

## Step 3 — Build exactly the relationships the marts were designed for

```
dim_locations[location_id]  1 ───── *  member_activity_mart[location_id]
dim_locations[location_id]  1 ───── *  revenue_mart[location_id]
```

Set both relationships to single-direction, filtering from `dim_locations` outward. Do not relate `member_activity_mart` to `revenue_mart` directly — they share a grain (location + month) but joining them in the model risks a fanout almost identical in shape to the billing-events bug fixed earlier in this series. If a visual needs both, it filters through `dim_locations`, not a direct mart-to-mart relationship.

## Step 4 — Write measures that quote the mart, not reinterpret it

```dax
Active Members =
CALCULATE (
    COUNTROWS ( member_activity_mart ),
    member_activity_mart[was_active_any_day] = TRUE
)

Net Revenue =
SUM ( revenue_mart[net_revenue] )

Revenue per Active Member =
DIVIDE ( [Net Revenue], [Active Members], 0 )
```

Every measure here is a direct aggregation of a column the mart already computed. None of them re-expresses the active-member rule or the revenue aggregation logic — that reasoning lives in `int_active_members` and the mart models, once, and Power BI simply reports it.

## Step 5 — Validate one measure by hand before building a single visual

Run this in Snowflake and compare it to the DAX card showing `[Active Members]` filtered to the same location and month:

```sql
select location_id, count_if(was_active_any_day) as active_members
from marts.member_activity_mart
where activity_month = '2026-09-01'
group by location_id
order by location_id;
```

If the Power BI card and this query don't match to the row, stop — something in the model, likely a relationship direction or an unwanted filter, is altering the number before it's displayed, and that has to be fixed before anyone sees this report.

## Step 6 — Set a retirement date for the three legacy reports

Publish the new workspace, share it with Finance's, Marketing's, and Product's leads, and put a specific decommission date — not "soon" — on the three old PBIX files, with their owners notified directly. A new, correct report sitting next to three old, wrong ones doesn't fix the trust problem; it just gives people four numbers to choose from instead of three.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Rebuilt the Power BI semantic model directly on member_activity_mart and revenue_mart in Import mode, with single-direction relationships through dim_locations. Every measure is a straight aggregation of a mart column — no DAX re-derives the active-member rule, so there's exactly one place that logic lives. Validated the Active Members card against a Snowflake query by hand before building any visuals, and we've got a hard decommission date set for Finance's, Marketing's, and Product's three legacy reports.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Power BI is now wired to the same governed data everyone agreed on, not three separate homemade queries. We've set a specific retirement date for the three old reports so we don't end up with four conflicting numbers instead of three — the whole point was to get down to one.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Finance, Marketing, and Product are about to look at the exact same dashboard, built on the data we already tested and fixed. The three old reports that started this whole conversation have a retirement date on them, so there's no path back to three different numbers.

lessons.title: Presenting the New Single Source of Truth to Three Teams
lessons.summary: The room where Finance, Marketing, and Product see one active-member number together for the first time — and the honest explanation for why it doesn't match any of their old ones.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the meeting the whole project has been building toward: Finance, Marketing, and Product in one room, looking at the same Power BI report at the same time, for the first time in the company's history. It does not go perfectly — the new active-member number is different from all three teams' old numbers, including, awkwardly, lower than what Marketing had been reporting to leadership for two quarters. That moment is the actual subject of this video.

The skill here isn't building anything new technically — it's explaining a number that disagrees with what three rooms of people already believed, using the real mechanics behind each gap — a genuine difference in definitions for the member count, and a real, already-fixed pipeline bug for the revenue dollars — instead of just asserting the new numbers are correct and asking everyone to trust them.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine three kids each think they know how tall a tree is, because each one measured it a different way — one walked it off in footsteps, one guessed by eye, one used a bent ruler. Then someone brings an actual tape measure, checked against a ruler known to be accurate, and the real height doesn't match any of their three guesses. Nobody was lying — they just each measured it a different way, and one of their rulers turns out to have been bent.

That's this meeting. Finance, Marketing, and Product each had their own number for how many members are active, and none of those numbers match the new, carefully checked one. The job isn't to make anyone feel wrong — it's to show exactly where each old number came from, and exactly why the new one is more trustworthy.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The mechanics of this meeting matter more than the slides. The right structure is to present the new numbers first, without apology, and then walk backward from each one to every team's old number using a reconciliation bridge — a literal accounting of the gap, not a hand-wave — and to keep the two kinds of gap separate rather than blurring them into one vague "the numbers changed" story. Marketing's old active-member count was taken as a month-end snapshot — membership status as of the last day of the month — which quietly misses anyone who was genuinely active for three weeks and paused before the month closed, where the governed rule counts a member active for the month if they were active on even one day within it. Finance's old active-member count used a billing-presence rule instead of a status-based one, which drifts in the other direction: it picks up a member billed a final prorated charge after their status had already moved to cancelled, and misses a small number of comped or free members who are status ACTIVE but never billed at all.

Finance's revenue number has a separate, more uncomfortable problem: their query joined against the billing-events table without aggregating it to one row per member per month first, so a member with a retry or a mid-month plan change had their charge summed more than once — the exact fanout bug fixed earlier in this project, now caught by a regression test if it ever recurs. The discipline under pressure is refusing to say "trust me, it's fixed now" and instead showing the mechanism for each gap on its own terms: the actual logic that caused each old number to drift, the actual dbt test that now catches a recurrence, and one real member whose day-level activity makes the definition concrete. A room full of people who've each been burned by a wrong number doesn't update on confidence — it updates on being shown the gears.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Prepare two reconciliation bridges before the meeting, not during it

The active-member count and the revenue number broke for different reasons. Keep them as two separate pieces of arithmetic rather than one vague "the numbers changed" story — and anchor both to the exact figures already proven in Lessons 15 and 16, not new ones invented for this meeting:

```
ACTIVE MEMBERS, SEPTEMBER

THE GOVERNED NUMBER (member_activity_mart, active on >= 1 day in
September): 43,588 -- this is Lesson 15's own figure, cross-checked
there against Finance's Sept-30 snapshot query (41,920) at the same
single-day grain, where the two matched exactly.

MARKETING'S OLD NUMBER:        41,100 active members
  (a month-end-only snapshot: membership_status = 'active' as of
   Sept 30, read off a single flag with no day-level history behind it)
  + 2,488  members who were genuinely active for part of September but
           had already paused or cancelled by the 30th -- missed,
           because a single end-of-month flag can only ever see the
           last day, never the weeks before it
  = 43,588  THE GOVERNED NUMBER

FINANCE'S OLD NUMBER:          44,230 active members
  (a billing-presence rule: anyone billed in the last 30 days)
  - 830   members billed one final prorated charge after their status
          had already moved to CANCELLED -- counted as active by a
          billing-presence rule, incorrectly
  + 188   comped/free members whose status is ACTIVE but who are never
          billed at all -- missed entirely by a billing-presence rule
  = 43,588  THE GOVERNED NUMBER
```

```
NET REVENUE, SEPTEMBER

WHAT revenue_mart WAS SHOWING (the bug, before Lesson 16's fix):
  $37,966,830
  - a join matching one invoice against every calendar day of its
    billing period instead of once, inflating the total by roughly
    29.5x -- the exact mechanism Lesson 16 diagnosed and fixed
  = $1,285,340  WHAT revenue_mart SHOWS NOW -- matches a hand-sum of
    the raw billing records exactly, per Lesson 15's own spot-check
```

Having both pieces of arithmetic ready, separately, and tied to numbers this room has already seen proven in earlier lessons, is what turns "the numbers changed" from a credibility problem into two documented, specific explanations.

## Step 2 — Open with the numbers, not an apology

```
"Here are the two numbers all three of your reports will show going
forward: 43,588 active members and $1,285,340 in net revenue for
September. I know both are different from what your teams have been
reporting, and I want to walk through exactly why, rather than just
asking you to trust them."
```

## Step 3 — Walk the room through the actual mechanism, using one real row

```sql
-- One real example worth projecting live: a member Marketing's
-- month-end snapshot missed, that the governed monthly rule catches
select member_id, activity_month, days_active, was_active_any_day
from marts.member_activity_mart
where member_id = 'MBR-10452' and activity_month = '2026-09-01';

-- days_active: 22   was_active_any_day: TRUE
-- active most of the month, paused on September 28th -- a snapshot
-- taken on the 30th would have missed this member entirely
```

Showing one concrete member, by ID, with their real day-level activity, does more to earn trust than any slide of aggregate numbers.

## Step 4 — Name the revenue bug directly, without minimizing it

```
"Part of the gap on Finance's revenue number was a real bug in our
pipeline, not a change in how we're counting -- a join against billing
events was summing some members' charges more than once in a month.
It's fixed, there's now an automated test that would catch it again,
and I can show you that test."
```

Naming a real, already-fixed bug plainly is more credible than implying the old number was simply wrong for an unspecified reason.

## Step 5 — Have Product's answer ready too, even though their gap is smaller

Product's old 14-day app check-in number was closer to the governed figure than Finance's or Marketing's, but it still doesn't match, and "it was already close" is not the same as "it was right" — a member who pays reliably but hasn't opened the app in three weeks is still active by the billing-based definition, and that distinction is worth stating out loud so Product doesn't walk away assuming their old logic was basically fine:

```
PRODUCT'S OLD NUMBER:          42,900 active members
  - app check-ins miss paying members who simply haven't opened the
    app recently, and separately count a small number of members who
    opened the app during a free trial that never converted to billing
  = 43,588  THE GOVERNED NUMBER
```

## Step 6 — Rehearse the two questions that will come up, before they do

```
Q: "If the number is lower than what we told our VP last quarter, do
    we have to restate that?"
A: "That's a real conversation to have, and it's better to have it now,
    deliberately, than to have someone notice the discrepancy later
    without this explanation attached. I can put together exactly what
    changed between then and now if that helps the conversation."

Q: "How do we know this number won't need correcting again in three
    months?"
A: "Two reasons: the bug that caused Finance's gap now has an automated
    test that fails the build if it recurs, and the definition itself
    is written down in a shared dictionary so it can't quietly drift
    the way it did across your three old queries."
```

Answering both before anyone has to ask them is what keeps this meeting feeling like a correction rather than a confrontation.

## Step 7 — Agree on ownership, not just the number

Close by getting explicit agreement that `member_activity_mart` and `revenue_mart` are now the source every team's reporting pulls from, and that any future change to the active-member definition goes through a documented change process, previewed in the next lesson's exposures, not a quiet edit to one team's query.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran the three-team reconciliation. Prepped separate numeric bridges for the active-member count and the revenue number, walked the room through one real member's day-level activity live, and named the revenue fanout bug directly rather than talking around it. Left with explicit agreement that member_activity_mart and revenue_mart are now the source of truth for all three teams.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Got Finance, Marketing, and Product in the same room looking at the same number for the first time. It didn't match any of their old reports, and instead of that landing as a credibility problem, we walked through exactly why for each team, with real numbers. All three teams signed off on adopting the new dashboard going forward.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Finance, Marketing, and Product now agree on one active-member number, and more importantly, they understand why it's different from what each of them had before — including a real pipeline bug we found and fixed ourselves. That's a stronger foundation than just picking a number and asking everyone to believe it.

lessons.title: Writing the Handoff Docs: dbt Docs, Exposures, and a Metrics Dictionary
lessons.summary: Generating dbt's own documentation site, declaring Power BI's dependency on the marts through exposures, and writing a metrics dictionary entry a non-technical stakeholder can actually trust.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The semantic layer is built, tested, presented, and adopted — now it needs to survive without you standing next to it. This video builds the three documents that make that possible: the dbt-generated documentation site, a set of `exposures:` entries that formally declare which Power BI reports depend on which marts, and a plain-English metrics dictionary entry for "Active Member" that Finance, Marketing, and Product can each reread on their own, months from now, without asking you what it means.

These three documents do different jobs. dbt docs answers "what does this model do, and where does its data come from." Exposures answer "if I change this model, what breaks downstream." The metrics dictionary answers the question a non-technical stakeholder actually asks, which isn't about models or tables at all — it's "what, exactly, counts as an active member, and can I trust that definition?"
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine you build a really good treehouse with a rulebook taped inside explaining how everything works, a sign on the ladder saying "if you move this ladder, the tire swing on the other side stops working," and a one-page note for grown-ups explaining the rules in plain words instead of carpenter talk. That's what this video is building for the data pipeline: a rulebook, warning signs about what's connected to what, and a plain note anyone can read.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The exposures feature exists specifically to solve the blast-radius problem that every analytics engineering team eventually hits: a model gets changed for a good reason, and three dashboards nobody remembered depending on it quietly break. Declaring Power BI reports as `exposures:` in dbt turns an invisible dependency into a visible one — `dbt docs generate` renders them directly in the lineage graph, so a developer about to change `int_active_members` sees, before merging, that Finance's, Marketing's, and Product's dashboards all sit downstream of it.

The metrics dictionary is a different kind of artifact entirely — it deliberately contains zero SQL, because its reader is not a developer. A good entry states the business rule in plain language, states what it explicitly excludes, since that's usually where the old misunderstandings lived, and states who owns changing it. Writing it well is as real a piece of engineering work as the dbt model itself: a correct model with an ambiguous or missing plain-English definition will still get silently reinterpreted by the next analyst who touches it.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Generate and serve dbt's own documentation site

```bash
dbt docs generate
dbt docs serve --port 8080
```

This builds a static site from the project's models, tests, and YAML descriptions, including a full lineage graph from `raw.sql_server_memberships` through `stg_memberships`, into `int_active_members`, out to `member_activity_mart` and `revenue_mart`. Confirm every model in that chain has a `description:` in its `.yml` file — an undocumented model shows up in the graph as a blank node, which defeats the point of generating this at all.

## Step 2 — Declare the Power BI reports as exposures

```yaml
# models/marts/exposures.yml
exposures:
  - name: finance_active_members_dashboard
    label: "Finance - Active Members & Revenue"
    type: dashboard
    maturity: high
    url: https://app.powerbi.com/groups/me/reports/finance-active-members
    description: >
      Finance's primary monthly active-member and revenue report.
      Replaces the legacy billing-events query retired in Lesson 17.
    depends_on:
      - ref('member_activity_mart')
      - ref('revenue_mart')
    owner:
      name: Brightleaf Finance Team
      email: finance-reporting@brightleaffitness.com

  - name: marketing_member_dashboard
    label: "Marketing - Member Activity"
    type: dashboard
    maturity: high
    depends_on:
      - ref('member_activity_mart')
    owner:
      name: Brightleaf Marketing Team
      email: marketing-analytics@brightleaffitness.com
```

With this committed, `dbt docs generate` shows both dashboards as downstream nodes directly on `member_activity_mart`'s lineage graph — anyone about to change that model sees, before they touch it, exactly which dashboards they could be about to break.

## Step 3 — Write the metrics dictionary entry for "Active Member"

```
METRIC: Active Member
DEFINITION: A member counts as active on a given day if their
            highest-priority membership status that day is ACTIVE.
            A member with overlapping memberships, such as a mid-month
            location transfer, is counted once, with ACTIVE preferred
            on any same-day tie. At the monthly grain Finance,
            Marketing, and Product all report from, a member is active
            for the month if they were active on at least one day
            within it.
WHAT THIS EXCLUDES: A snapshot taken only as of month-end misses a
            member who was active for most of the month and paused
            a few days before it closed -- the day-level rule, not a
            single snapshot, decides the month's flag, which is why
            this number can come in higher than a month-end-only read.
WHERE IT LIVES: marts.member_activity_mart, column was_active_any_day.
            The day-level rule itself is defined once, in
            int_active_members -- not recalculated anywhere else.
LAST CHANGED: see Lesson 10, where the day-spine expansion and the
            same-day tie-break rule were written.
OWNER: Analytics Engineering. Changing this definition requires sign-off
       from Finance, Marketing, and Product -- the three teams who
       agreed to adopt it as their shared source of truth.
```

## Step 4 — Write a second dictionary entry so the pattern is obviously repeatable

One entry can look like a one-off nicety. A second one, for a metric that genuinely needed the same treatment, proves the format itself is the deliverable, not just the single definition:

```
METRIC: Net Revenue
DEFINITION: Gross billing amount collected from a member in a given
            month, minus refunds and failed-charge reversals for that
            same month. Aggregated once per member per month before
            being summed across members or locations.
WHAT THIS EXCLUDES: Does NOT include one-time merchandise or personal-
            training add-on purchases -- those are tracked separately
            and were never part of this project's scope.
WHY THE AGGREGATION STEP MATTERS: Summing billing events directly,
            without first collapsing to one row per member per month,
            previously double-counted members with a retry or a plan
            change in a given month -- the exact bug fixed earlier in
            this series. revenue_mart performs that aggregation before
            any join, which is what keeps this number correct.
WHERE IT LIVES: marts.revenue_mart, column net_revenue.
OWNER: Analytics Engineering, with Finance as the primary reviewer for
       any change to the refund or reversal logic.
```

## Step 5 — Walk the three stakeholder teams through where to find all of it

Don't assume a committed file and a hosted docs link are self-explanatory. Spend fifteen minutes with a representative from each of Finance, Marketing, and Product showing them, live, exactly where the metrics dictionary lives, how to open the dbt docs lineage graph for `member_activity_mart`, and who to contact if a number ever looks wrong. This is the same handoff discipline as the earlier reconciliation meeting: a document nobody was shown how to use might as well not exist.

## Step 6 — Store all three documents where the next person will actually find them

Commit `exposures.yml` into the dbt project itself, publish the dbt docs output somewhere the whole analytics org can reach without a local `dbt docs serve` session, a hosted docs site or a CI artifact, and put the metrics dictionary in the same shared space Finance, Marketing, and Product already use for other definitions — not a personal notes file. A document that only you can find isn't really a handoff.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Generated dbt docs with full lineage from the raw SQL Server tables through to both marts, added exposures.yml declaring Finance's and Marketing's Power BI dashboards as explicit downstream dependents, and wrote the Active Member metrics dictionary entry defining exactly what it excludes. Anyone touching int_active_members now sees the dashboard blast radius before they merge, not after something breaks.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've documented not just how the pipeline works, but what depends on it and what 'active member' actually means in plain language. That means a future change to this logic gets caught before it breaks someone's dashboard, instead of becoming a surprise support ticket.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've written down, in plain language, exactly what counts as an active member and who's allowed to change that definition. That protects the trust we just built in the last meeting — the definition can't quietly drift again without everyone agreeing first.

lessons.title: Wrap-Up: What Changed, and What's Still Manual
lessons.summary: The honest closing assessment of the whole Brightleaf Fitness build — what's genuinely solved, and what's still manual, fragile, or deferred.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the last video in the series, and it isn't a highlight reel. Over nineteen lessons, Brightleaf Fitness went from three teams arguing over three different "active member" numbers to one governed, tested, version-controlled semantic layer that Finance, Marketing, and Product all now query from — a real pipeline running nightly from legacy SQL Server through Python and Airflow into Snowflake, through dbt staging, intermediate, and mart models, enforced by dbt tests and a CI pipeline, and surfaced in one Power BI model with documentation and exposures behind it. That part is real and it's done.

What this video does instead of celebrating is the harder, more useful thing: naming exactly what's still manual, still fragile, or still a single point of failure, so whoever maintains this platform next — possibly you, six months from now — isn't caught off guard by a limitation that was always there but never said out loud.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you spent weeks building a really solid treehouse — strong boards, a good ladder, a roof that doesn't leak. It's genuinely great. But a good builder doesn't just say "it's perfect, goodbye" — they say "this part is solid, but that board still needs checking every few months, and if the old tree it's built on ever gets sick, that's a bigger problem no treehouse fix solves." That honesty is what makes the treehouse actually safe to keep using, instead of someone discovering its limits the hard way later.

That's this whole video: being straight about what's genuinely solid in what we built, and what still needs a human checking in on it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A credible project retrospective does two things most victory-lap wrap-ups skip: it states the real architecture plainly enough that someone who missed the first nineteen videos could still understand what's running, and it enumerates the actual gaps with the same specificity the earlier lessons used for bugs — not "there's room for improvement," but named, concrete limitations. For Brightleaf, three are worth stating without softening: there is no automated data-quality alerting beyond what CI catches on a pull request, so a bad value that lands in production between deploys, inside already-merged logic, has no monitor watching for it until someone notices a number looks wrong; there is no self-service metrics layer or BI-agnostic semantic tool, so a team that wants a number outside Power BI still has to either query the marts directly in SQL or ask analytics engineering, a real, if smaller, version of the original problem; and the legacy SQL Server instance remains the one irreplaceable upstream source — if it goes down or its schema changes unexpectedly, the entire nightly pipeline has nothing to extract from, and no amount of dbt testing downstream protects against that.

Naming these isn't an admission of failure — overselling a system's completeness to a stakeholder is itself a trust problem, the same category of problem this whole project started by fixing. The honest version of "done" is "this solved the specific, real problem we scoped, these are its real edges, and here's what a future phase would need to address them."
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — State the finished architecture in one pass, end to end

```
SOURCE:        Legacy SQL Server (memberships, billing, locations)
EXTRACT:       Nightly Python script, orchestrated by Airflow
LANDING:       raw.sql_server_memberships / _billing / _locations in Snowflake
TRANSFORM:     dbt staging (stg_memberships, stg_billing, stg_locations)
               -> dbt intermediate (int_active_members -- the one place
                  "active member" is defined)
               -> dbt marts (member_activity_mart, revenue_mart)
TESTED BY:     dbt generic + custom singular tests, run in CI on every PR
ORCHESTRATED:  Airflow DAG, nightly
SURFACED IN:   One Power BI semantic model, Import mode, shared by
               Finance, Marketing, and Product
DOCUMENTED BY: dbt docs, exposures.yml, and a plain-English metrics
               dictionary
```

Every box in that chain was built, tested, and is now in use by all three teams -- that's the real, defensible claim this project gets to make.

## Step 2 — Name what's still manual, specifically

```
GAP 1: No automated data-quality alerting beyond CI.
  dbt tests only run when a PR triggers CI. A bad value that enters
  through already-merged, already-passing logic -- a billing system
  change, a new edge case in the source data -- has no monitor
  watching production runs between deploys. Someone has to notice a
  number looks wrong and go investigate, the same way the billing-fanout
  bug was originally found: by a human looking closely, not an alert.

GAP 2: No self-service metrics layer.
  "Active Member" and the core revenue measures are defined once, well,
  in dbt -- but only Power BI and direct SQL against the marts can use
  that definition today. A team wanting the number in a spreadsheet or
  a different tool either queries the marts directly or asks analytics
  engineering for an export, a smaller-scale version of the original
  three-queries problem if it's allowed to spread informally.

GAP 3: Legacy SQL Server is still the single point of failure.
  Every mart, every test, every dashboard ultimately depends on one
  aging on-premises database staying up and keeping a stable schema.
  No amount of downstream dbt testing protects against that system
  going down or changing shape without notice -- it protects everything
  built on top of it, not the foundation itself.
```

## Step 3 — Write the honest one-paragraph summary for whoever reads this next

```
"This project replaced three conflicting ad-hoc queries with one
governed, tested semantic layer that Finance, Marketing, and Product
all now use, and fixed a real revenue-counting bug along the way. It
did not add production alerting beyond CI, a self-service metrics
tool, or a plan for the legacy SQL Server source's own reliability --
those are real, named gaps for a future phase, not oversights we're
pretending don't exist."
```

## Step 4 — Leave a short, prioritized list for "if there's a phase two"

```
1. Production data-quality monitoring (scheduled dbt test runs with
   alerting, independent of CI) -- closes Gap 1, highest value for
   the lowest lift.
2. Evaluate a semantic-layer tool so non-Power-BI consumers can query
   governed metrics directly -- closes Gap 2.
3. A migration plan or at minimum a documented contingency for the
   legacy SQL Server source -- closes Gap 3, hardest and most expensive.
```

That's the real, unglamorous ending: not every problem solved, but every remaining one named, owned, and ready to hand to whoever picks this up next.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Closed the series with the full architecture laid out end to end — SQL Server through Airflow, Snowflake, dbt's staging/intermediate/mart layers, CI-enforced tests, and the Power BI model with its exposures and docs. Named three real gaps rather than glossing over them: no production data-quality alerting beyond CI, no self-service metrics layer outside Power BI and direct SQL, and legacy SQL Server remaining the one true single point of failure upstream of everything we built.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Wrapped the project with an honest accounting of what shipped versus what's still open. Finance, Marketing, and Product are genuinely unified on one number now — that part is real and done. We've also got a prioritized, named list of what a phase two would need to tackle, so nothing gets rediscovered as a surprise later.
workplaceExplanation.executive: What we built is real: one trusted number, used by all three teams, with a bug fixed along the way that was quietly affecting revenue reporting. We're also telling you plainly what this doesn't cover yet — ongoing automatic monitoring, a tool for teams outside Power BI, and the fact that the old SQL Server system underneath all of this is still a risk we haven't solved. That's the honest finish line, not an oversold one.
